name: Delphi (Digital Mind)
what: Creators build a chatbot 'digital mind' from their books, articles, podcasts, YouTube and courses; hosted free and paid tiers, REST API top tier only.
why_it_matters: Closest commercial analogue to a person-as-advisor; the cited-answer claim is from third-party reviews, not the product page.
numbers: Pricing conflicts across third-party sources: $79/mo creators and $299/mo leaders (startupsignals substack); creator plans from ~$19 (tooldirectory.ai) or $29 (other directory); Matthew Hussey clone $39/mo. Source: https://startupsignals.substack.com/p/delphi-can-you-package-a-mind
note: grounding: creator corpus RAG (claimed); cites: claimed by reviews only; refuses: not verified; consent: creator self-serve, terms not read

name: Dexa (Huberman AI search)
what: AI search over podcast transcripts; returns an AI summary plus pointers to episodes and timestamped links; began as Huberman-focused tool, now multi-podcast.
why_it_matters: Best live example of a summary-with-timestamped-source UI on one person's catalogue; shows citation-by-link but no published refusal rule.
numbers: 120+ podcasts indexed (TechCrunch, 5 Feb 2024); $6M seed (BetaKit); no revenue then, subscriptions and ads considered. Source: https://techcrunch.com/2024/02/05/dexa-aims-to-get-more-out-of-podcasts-with-ai-powered-search
note: grounding: transcript search + summary; cites: yes, timestamped episode links; refuses: not stated; consent: Huberman Lab partnership, free access for listeners

name: Character.AI (celebrity and likeness bots)
what: Hosts user-made bots of real figures (e.g. Nicki Minaj, Elon Musk, Donald Trump per search coverage); removals happen after complaints, rightsholder letters or press inquiries, not proactive.
why_it_matters: Shows the default for person bots is complaint-driven takedown; the stated impersonation clause could not be re-verified.
numbers: Garcia and four other teen-harm suits settled Jan 2026, terms undisclosed (citizen.digital). Disney C&D removals were partial (NBC News).
note: grounding: none (roleplay); cites: no; refuses: no; consent: no published public-figure permission process found; ConductAtlas says impersonation clause no longer published, correction CR-002704 flags it unverifiable

name: Meta AI celebrity personas (discontinued)
what: Celebrity-licensed chat personas (Snoop Dogg, Tom Brady, Kendall Jenner); played archetypes, not the celebrity's own voice or record; shut down or de-celebritied within about a year.
why_it_matters: Failure case for celebrity likeness deals: low engagement despite fees; a benchmark for why a person-advisor needs a grounded corpus, not a persona.
numbers: Reported up to $5M per celebrity likeness fee and low follower uptake (Digital Trends, TechRadar; press reports, not Meta disclosures).
note: grounding: persona prompt; cites: no; refuses: no; consent: licensed likeness fees

name: Hello History
what: One-on-one chats with AI-generated historical figures; app store product; no citation feature and no accuracy disclaimer on the research page.
why_it_matters: Contrast case: persona chat for dead figures with no disclosed sourcing; not a corpus-grounded advisor.
numbers: Subscription $2 to $35/month, free tier (topai.tools listing, unverified against store). Source: https://topai.tools/s/history-ai
note: grounding: none disclosed; cites: no; refuses: no; consent: n/a (historical figures)

name: Essays by Paul Graham GPT (third-party custom GPT)
what: Third-party custom GPT that answers only from paulgraham.com essays and cites them; built because GPT was guessing what PG would say. Not official.
why_it_matters: Closest public match to our spec (corpus-only plus cites), but reliance on the model's answer discipline is untested.
numbers: Corpus size disputed: 1200+ pages / 500k words vs curated 200+ essays (listings, aipure.ai and productcool). Requires ChatGPT Plus per listing.
note: grounding: essay RAG (custom GPT); cites: claimed yes; refuses: not verified; consent: author not involved (public essays)

name: Ask Naval / Naval AI (fan bots)
what: Fan-made bots not affiliated with Naval Ravikant; trained on tweets, interviews and The Almanack of Naval Ravikant (Eric Jorgenson); answers in his style.
why_it_matters: Shows the default for popular advisors: mixed corpus, style-mimicry, no disclosed citations, no author endorsement.
numbers: No pricing or usage numbers found in listings (creati.ai, toolify, logicweb).
note: grounding: mixed corpus plus model; cites: no; refuses: no; consent: none, unaffiliated

name: StoryFile (interactive oral history)
what: Subject records answers to many pre-scripted questions; visitors ask questions and the system retrieves a matching clip. It never generates new speech. Museum deployments include Holocaust survivor testimony.
why_it_matters: The strongest existing pattern for quote-only fidelity: retrieval over recorded verbatim answers, with a fallback to the closest recorded question and operator override.
numbers: One museum estimate about $250,000 per subject (recording, interface, education) (press coverage, 2023 era). Matching errors were seen at live events.
note: grounding: pre-recorded answers retrieved, no generation; cites: clip-level; refuses: redirects to closest question; consent: subject records own answers

name: HereAfter AI
what: Person records life stories with the company before death; family can then talk to an avatar built from those recordings. Subject signs an agreement before death.
why_it_matters: Clearest opt-in model for a post-mortem advisor: consent captured from the subject while alive.
numbers: Plans from USD 39 per year (2022 commentary). Current terms not checked.
note: grounding: subject's own recordings; cites: not found; refuses: not found; consent: subject signs pre-death agreement

name: Rai 1 Ipazia (AI avatar on Codice)
what: AI avatar on Rai 1's Codice that answers live over a retrieval system on the show's archive. It is a fictional branded avatar named after Hypatia, not a real person.
why_it_matters: Broadcaster pattern: archive RAG with on-air answers; a template for a corpus-bounded advisor on TV.
numbers: Debut episode 4 Sep 2026; RAG over about a decade of archive (single blog source, no Rai release found).
note: grounding: archive RAG (claimed); cites: not stated; refuses: not stated; consent: not a real person

name: ElevenLabs Iconic Marketplace
what: Marketplace where licensed celebrity voices (e.g. Michael Caine, Matthew McConaughey as investor) are approved for brand use; rights holders approve each script.
why_it_matters: Live model of opt-in, per-use consent for a living person's likeness with approval rights; relevant to any advisor that uses a real voice.
numbers: Script review within average 72 hours (company announcement, Nov 2025); no license fee published (press); terms set per deal.
note: grounding: voice model, no corpus Q&A; cites: no; refuses: approval gate; consent: opt-in license, per-use approval, negotiated terms

name: Sensay (digital replicas)
what: London startup making 'replicas' trained on a person's documents, video, interviews and email; has a hallucination warning flag on answers that rely on assumed information; proof-of-humanity link.
why_it_matters: Only product found with an explicit per-answer 'not from source' flag, which is half of our refusal rule.
numbers: Founder claim 90% to 95% indistinguishable (Thomson, unverified). NFT minting per replica (press release).
note: grounding: multi-source persona RAG; cites: hallucination flag not citations; refuses: flags assumed content; consent: proof-of-humanity

name: Personal.ai
what: Personal memory and digital twin that stores a user's messages, notes and documents as memory stacks.
why_it_matters: Pricing and memory model for a self-owned advisor; no evidence found of answer-only-from-data or per-answer citations.
numbers: Individual $40/mo or $400/yr, 50k memory cap, 10k messages; enterprise from $1,000/mo (undated pricing snapshot via search summary, verify). Source: https://www.personal.ai/insights
note: grounding: personal memory store; cites: not found; refuses: not found; consent: owner controls own data (company claim)

name: Amazon Kindle Ask This Book
what: Always-on AI Q&A inside Kindle books, live on some devices since Dec 2025; publishers and authors cannot opt out.
why_it_matters: Live example of an author's book answering questions with no consent gate; the Authors Guild dispute is the consent precedent for any book-based advisor.
numbers: No opt-out (Amazon spokesperson via Writer Beware, Dec 2025). Authors Guild statement is primary.
note: grounding: book text RAG; cites: not confirmed; refuses: not confirmed; consent: none, no opt-out

name: BBC Maestro Agatha Christie Writing (AI version)
what: Online writing course taught by an AI version of Christie built from her texts and interviews, approved by the estate; criticised for consent of the dead.
why_it_matters: Estate-approved post-mortem persona; shows estate sign-off does not settle the ethics objection.
numbers: Price $89 (NYT via press). Course is about 2.5 hours (Killzone blog).
note: grounding: estate texts (paraphrase disputed); cites: no; refuses: no; consent: estate approval, Veliz says the dead cannot consent

name: Replika / Luka Inc. Garante fine (incident)
what: Italy's data authority fined Luka Inc. EUR 5 million for no valid legal basis, a privacy notice that did not explain purposes or rights, and weak age checks.
why_it_matters: Regulatory precedent for companion or persona bots under GDPR: legal basis and minors, not likeness.
numbers: EUR 5M fine announced 19 May 2025 (press); earlier processing limit Feb 2023.
note: grounding: n/a; cites: n/a; refuses: n/a; consent: GDPR legal basis and age gate, not emotional consent

name: NPR: AI deadbots, Parkland case
what: Overview of AI deadbots of dead people, including a Parkland shooting victim's likeness used in court; researchers warn deadbots are primed for monetisation and persuasion.
why_it_matters: Incident evidence that deadbots are used in legal and public settings without the subject's consent.
numbers: Only search snippet read (fetch timed out); no figures used.
note: grounding: n/a; cites: n/a; refuses: n/a; consent: none for the dead

name: Generative Agent Simulations of 1,000 People (Park et al.)
what: Agents grounded in 2-hour qualitative interviews of 1,052 Americans, scored on held-out GSS, personality and economic-game answers.
why_it_matters: Best evidence that an interview-grounded persona tracks a real person; the paper does not test refusal or citation.
numbers: Normalized accuracy vs participants own 2-week retest: interview-only 83%, survey-only 82%, combined 86%, demographics-only 74% (arXiv abstract page, v3 28 Jun 2026).
note: grounding: interview transcript in prompt; cites: no; refuses: not tested; consent: participants consented to research; HAI flags privacy and misuse | check: arXiv 2411.10109 v3 (28 Jun 2026): 1,052 Americans; interview-only 83%, survey-only 82%, combined 86%, demographics-only 74%, all relative to participants' own 2-week retest. Abstract does not use the phrase 'normalized accuracy'.

name: ALCE: Enabling LLMs to Generate Text with Citations (Gao et al., EMNLP 2023)
what: First benchmark for citation evaluation (ASQA, QAMPARI, ELI5); scores fluency, correctness and citation quality.
why_it_matters: Standard metric for our cite-every-sentence rule; the citation-recall definition is what we should copy.
numbers: On ELI5 the best models lack complete citation support about 50% of the time (version-dependent: 49 generations in v1 abstract). Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14627
note: grounding: retrieval then cited generation; cites: metric; refuses: not in scope; consent: n/a | check: arXiv 2305.14627 abstract: on ELI5 'even the best models lack complete citation support 50% of the time'. Matches. The '49 generations in v1' detail was not visible on the abstract page.

name: TwinVoice (benchmark for LLM digital twins of specific people)
what: Benchmark for whether LLMs can act as convincing digital twins of specific people; scores mindset coherence and linguistic expression.
why_it_matters: Only persona-to-real-person benchmark found; can measure how our advisor matches a person's voice.
numbers: No figures read. arXiv ID not confirmed (aggregator cites Du et al., 29 Oct 2025).
note: grounding: n/a; cites: n/a; refuses: n/a; consent: n/a; primary paper not located

name: Quantifying and Optimizing Global Faithfulness in Persona-driven Role-playing (Peng and Shang)
what: Quantifies how faithful a role-play LLM is to a persona document and proposes a fine-grained faithfulness score.
why_it_matters: Metric for checking an answer stays inside the persona document; adaptable to a corpus.
numbers: No figures read in this pass.
note: grounding: persona doc; cites: no; refuses: no; consent: n/a

name: PersonaEval (who is speaking benchmark)
what: Tests whether LLM judges can identify which character is speaking, using novel, script and transcript dialogue.
why_it_matters: Shows models stay weak at telling a person apart from the persona; a check for our voice-fidelity eval.
numbers: Best LLMs about 69% accuracy vs about 90.8% for humans (per summary; verify in paper).
note: grounding: n/a; cites: n/a; refuses: n/a; consent: n/a; dialogue is fictional, not public statements

name: NO FAKES Act (S.1367 / H.R.2794)
what: Federal bill creating a property right in voice and visual likeness, with notice-and-takedown duties for platforms and a post-mortem right up to 70 years.
why_it_matters: Would govern any living or dead person's replica used in an advisor; still pending as of last search.
numbers: Reintroduced 9 Apr 2025 (Blackburn, Coons, Tillis, Klobuchar; Salazar, Dean). Post-mortem up to 70 years (Baker Botts, Regulatory Review). Status: committee.
note: law: federal likeness right, pending; platform liability on knowledge; state preemption carve-outs | check: Reintroduced April 2025 as S.1367 / H.R.2794 (Regulatory Review); post-mortem 'more than 70 years' for commercial use; still in committee and no later action found (congress.gov and govtrack returned 403/blocked).

name: Tennessee ELVIS Act
what: Adds voice to Tennessee's Personal Rights Protection Act; creates liability for tools whose primary purpose is unauthorised voice or likeness facsimiles.
why_it_matters: Only enacted US state law that reaches the voice and the tool maker; relevant to any voice-based advisor sold into Tennessee.
numbers: Signed 21 Mar 2024, effective 1 Jul 2024; misdemeanor plus private action; treble damages if knowing. Statute Tenn. Code Ann. 47-25-1101 et seq. (verify text).
note: law: voice right of publicity; tool liability; in force | check: Signed 21 Mar 2024 and effective 1 Jul 2024 confirmed (WSGR/Proskauer), private cause of action against tool distributors confirmed. Treble damages for knowing violations NOT found in fetched sources; remove or source it.

name: EU AI Act Article 50 (transparency duties)
what: Chatbot disclosure (50(1)) and deepfake disclosure (50(4)) apply from 2 Aug 2026; AI-generated public-interest text needs disclosure; machine-readable marking (50(2)) has a grace period for legacy systems.
why_it_matters: Binding EU disclosure duty for any advisor that speaks as a person or synthesises a real person; draft Commission guidelines pending.
numbers: Fines up to EUR 15M or 3% of global turnover (per CSA and law-firm summaries); 50(2) grace to 2 Dec 2026 for systems already on market.
note: law: disclosure of AI and of deepfakes; in force 2 Aug 2026; secondary sources, read Reg (EU) 2024/1689 | check: Article 50 applies from 2 Aug 2026 (artificialintelligenceact.eu confirms). Not confirmed: the 50(2) grace date 2 Dec 2026 (no source text found; the Nov 2025 Digital Omnibus proposal reportedly set about 2 Feb 2027, check adopted text). Fine ceiling EUR 15M/3% not on the fetched page (Art. 99 not read).

name: Wikidata
what: Open structured knowledge base; humans are items with instance-of Q5 and carry IDs for most other people databases.
why_it_matters: Backbone identifier hub for the people graph; most other rows here map to a Wikidata property.
numbers: Direct instance-of human: 6,376,879 items (2025 workshop page); with subclasses about 10.3M (older query page, 2018). Run the Q5 count yourself for a live figure.
ui_notes: Query service at query.wikidata.org (SPARQL); Special:Statistics for totals.
note: Counts disagree by method; the two sources are dated. | check: Wikidata SPARQL today: ?p wdt:P31 wd:Q5 returns 13,738,279 (row 6,376,879 is a stale 2025 figure, about half the live count).

name: Pantheon 1.0 (MIT Media Lab)
what: Manually verified dataset of globally famous biographies with birth data, gender, occupation taxonomy and popularity scores, built from Wikipedia language editions.
why_it_matters: Closest existing notability ranking for people; its popularity score and occupation taxonomy are reusable ranking signals.
numbers: 11,341 biographies appearing in 25+ Wikipedia languages (Scientific Data, PMC4700860).
ui_notes: Downloadable data and an online explorer; check for a newer Pantheon release before use.
note: Search returned only Pantheon 1.0 material; newer versions unconfirmed. Popularity is Wikipedia-based, which critics say is not universal fame. | check: PMC4700860 abstract: Pantheon 1.0 includes 11,341 biographies present in more than 25 Wikipedia languages; matches row.

name: Human Biographical Record (HBR), Nekoei and Sinn
what: Notable-people dataset with Wikidata as backbone and Wikipedia text from all 292 language editions.
why_it_matters: Large, multilingual notable-people base with text; a direct comparator for a people graph.
numbers: More than 7 million notable individuals (CEPR DP15825).
note: Access terms not checked.

name: Cross-verified Database of Notable People 3500BC-2018AD (Laouenan et al.)
what: Notable-people database built from Wikipedia and Wikidata editions with each field cross-checked across sources.
why_it_matters: Cross-verification method is the quality bar for merging person records.
numbers: More than 2 million individuals (search summary of Scientific Data 2022 paper).
note: The 2 million figure came from a search summary; confirm in the paper.

name: Notable people database (Gergaud et al., HAL)
what: Notable people extracted from Wikipedia biographies, with associated locations.
why_it_matters: Provides person-to-place links, which the people graph needs for geography.
numbers: 1,243,776 notable people and 7,184,575 associated locations (HAL record).
note: Titled A Brief History of Human Time.

name: Wiki people (Douwe Osinga)
what: Browsable database of people built from Wikidata, limited to humans with English Wikipedia articles, born 1500-2010.
why_it_matters: Working example of a people browser built on Wikidata that can be copied for UI ideas.
numbers: About 1.9 million people (project page, via search summary).
ui_notes: Browser-style person pages.
note: Hobby project; freshness unknown.

name: wikidata-bulk-people (PyPI)
what: Python tool that extracts structured person records from Wikipedia and Wikidata at scale to JSONL, CSV or SQL.
why_it_matters: Ready-made extractor for loading the people graph from dumps.
numbers: No counts given on the package page.
note: Read the source before running any package code.

name: FamilySearch Prominent Persons Index (Wikipedia)
what: US-focused index of notable people from Wikipedia with name, birth and death dates and places, and a link to the Wikipedia page.
why_it_matters: Genealogy-side notability index with date and place fields for matching.
numbers: Coverage 1500-2022 (collection page); record count not captured.
ui_notes: Search requires a FamilySearch login.
note: Login needed; not checked.

name: Wikiquote
what: Open quotation wiki with one page per person, licensed CC BY-SA, covering many languages.
why_it_matters: Main open source of attributed quotes per person, keyed to Wikidata.
numbers: About 168,000 articles in 89 languages as of 10 May 2014 (Meta-Wiki); current total not found.
ui_notes: MediaWiki API for access.
note: Count is from 2014; check the live statistics page.

name: Quote Garden API
what: Free REST API of famous quotes with author names.
why_it_matters: Cheap quote source to test attribution pipelines.
numbers: More than 5,000 quotes (publicapis.io listing).
note: License not checked; the listing links to the service rather than the provider.

name: They Said So Quotes API
what: Hosted quotes API with lookup by author, category or tag.
why_it_matters: Commercial quote-by-author source if Wikiquote coverage is thin.
numbers: Pricing not captured.
note: Commercial; check terms before use.

name: Iconic Quotes API (Zyla Labs)
what: Marketplace quotes API with a free trial and paid tiers.
why_it_matters: Another quote feed to compare for coverage and price.
numbers: Free trial of 3 test requests; Pro plan lists 10,000 calls (listing).
note: Listing copy reads like marketing; quote sources unverified.

name: IMDb Non-Commercial Datasets (name.basics)
what: Daily TSV dumps of IMDb titles and people, including name.basics with person ID, name, birth and death years, professions and known-for titles.
why_it_matters: Largest free film and TV people index with stable IDs (nconst) for linking.
numbers: Full set about 1 GB (pimdb docs); row counts for name.basics not captured.
note: Personal and non-commercial use only; the download host is datasets.imdbws.com.

name: Open Library (authors)
what: Internet Archive book catalog with author records, monthly bulk dumps and a JSON API.
why_it_matters: Open author records with IDs that link to Wikidata and VIAF.
numbers: About 6 million authors and over 20 million editions (site, via search summary).
note: Author endpoint paths not confirmed.

name: MusicBrainz
what: Open music metadata database with artist records typed as Person, Group and so on, plus full PostgreSQL dumps.
why_it_matters: Open artist IDs (MBIDs) with person typing, useful for musicians in the people graph.
numbers: 2,872,200 artists (May 2026 mirror statistics); about 53.7% typed Person (mirror page).
note: Figures are from third-party mirrors; confirm on musicbrainz.org. | check: musicbrainz.org/statistics (updated 2026-10-13): 3,012,034 artists (row 2,872,200, -4.7%, within 10%); Person 53.6% (row 53.7%).

name: ORCID
what: Registry of researcher identifiers with a free public API and an annual CC0 public data file.
why_it_matters: Authoritative researcher identity layer for authors and scientists.
numbers: Passed 10 million iDs in late 2020; annual public data file (2023 edition, CC0) (ORCID pages).
note: Live total not found; check the ORCID statistics page.

name: OpenAlex
what: Open index of works, authors, institutions and topics with a free REST API and full dumps.
why_it_matters: Largest open author-disambiguated index for scholars; useful for research people.
numbers: 2022 paper: 209M works and 2013M disambiguated authors (figure as reported; likely a typo, check); later counts higher (arXiv 2205.01833).
ui_notes: Free API key required.
note: Author disambiguation is the weakest area per the paper. | check: api.openalex.org today: 326,886,422 works and 96,474,526 authors; row's '2013M authors' is implausible (about 20x live) and the 209M works figure is out of date.

name: Discogs
what: Music marketplace and database with artist, label and release pages, plus monthly data dumps.
why_it_matters: Large crowd-built artist index, strong for electronic and vinyl artists.
numbers: Passed 5 million artists in 2017 and 10 million releases in 2018 (press milestones); dump sizes not captured.
note: Milestone figures are dated; check the data dumps page.

name: Find a Grave
what: User-built memorial database of burial sites and people, with bios and family links.
why_it_matters: Large dated-death index for people, and Wikidata P1036 links to it.
numbers: 13.7M memorials added in 2023 (site's own year review); about 180M entries in FamilySearch index (2019 blog).
note: Copyright and terms apply; the OSM wiki advises Wikidata over ref:find_a_grave.

name: Prabook
what: Free English biographical encyclopedia founded in 2018, with profile pages for professionals.
why_it_matters: Large professional-bio source for business and academic people.
numbers: Profile count not found.
note: Operator named as The World Biographic Encyclopedia, Inc. Check for terms before scraping.

name: Oxford Dictionary of National Biography
what: Authoritative UK biography reference with peer-reviewed lives and full-text search.
why_it_matters: High-quality bios for British and Commonwealth people, a quality benchmark for descriptions.
numbers: Over 60,000 lives (library pages); 54,922 lives in 50,113 articles in the 2005 print edition (ABR review).
ui_notes: Free to UK library members via library login.
note: Not open access; licensed.

name: Deutsche Biographie (NDB, ADB)
what: Online German biography database covering the NDB and ADB, with a name index of persons and families.
why_it_matters: Authoritative German-language biographies and an index with cross-links.

name: Notable Names Database (NNDB)
what: Biographical database with executive summaries, career timelines, and a visual connection mapper.
why_it_matters: Adds connection data between people, which is an edge type for the graph.
numbers: Over 40,000 people (search summary of Wikipedia-derived text).
ui_notes: NNDB Mapper (connections) since May 2008.
note: Status disputed: some sources say no updates since 2022.

name: Behind the Name
what: Given-name etymology database run since 1996 by one owner, covering names from many cultures and fiction.
why_it_matters: Name-to-meaning and gender metadata for name parsing in person records.
numbers: 30,549 names in the main database and 219,570 in the submitted database (About page).
note: Names, not people; included for name-parsing use.

name: The Movie Database (TMDB)
what: Film and TV database with person endpoints for cast and crew, birthdays, places of birth and images.

name: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires (via third-party scrapers)

numbers: Cost $0 (paper). Related: Aggazzotti et al. TACL 2025 (speaker attribution from language in ASR transcripts, EMNLP 2025 presentation); Gobara et al. 2025 LLM speaker-ID dataset construction ~90% LLM accuracy on Japanese narratives (not interviews).
ui_notes: Keep the attribution decision and confidence per quote in the record.
note: ToS/legal LOW (academic paper). Maintenance: static; no 2026 interview-specific paper found in this search.

name: Wikidata entity dumps directory (sizes)
what: Official Wikimedia listing of Wikidata entity dumps. Latest dated directory shown is 20261012.
why_it_matters: Sets disk and download budget for a humans+orgs T0 extract from the full dump instead of the live API.
numbers: latest-all.json.bz2 = 103,409,622,204 bytes (~103 GB); latest-truthy.nt.bz2 = 43,534,958,911 bytes (~43.5 GB); latest-all.nt.bz2 = 196,233,094,777 bytes (~196 GB); latest-all.ttl.bz2 = 125,778,820,821 bytes (~126 GB). Source: directory listing fetched 2026-10-14. Meta dump page says Jan 2026 uncompressed size 1.6 TB (https://meta.wikimedia.org/wiki/Data_dumps/Dumps_sizes_and_growth).
ui_notes: Pick latest-truthy.nt.bz2 for a smaller first pass (best-rank direct values only, no qualifiers); pick latest-all.json.bz2 when qualifiers or sitelinks are needed.
note: Sizes are compressed bytes from the directory listing; uncompressed is roughly 1.6 TB per Meta.

name: Wikidata:Database download (formats, tools, incremental)
what: Official page listing Wikidata dump formats, licence and third-party readers.
why_it_matters: Canonical source for CC0 licence of structured data and for the incremental-dump location.
numbers: JSON dumps are weekly; incremental dumps cover about one day each at https://dumps.wikimedia.org/other/incr/wikidatawiki/. Tools named on page: wdumper, qwikidata (Python), JsonDumpReader (PHP), gitlab.com/tozd/go/mediawiki (Go), WDSub (Scala), simple-wikidata-db (Python), wd2sql (Rust, JSON dump to SQLite). Page gives an academictorrents example of 130.53 GiB for wikidata-20240101-all.json.gz (fetched 2026-10-14).
note: wikidata-filter, KGTK and QLever are NOT mentioned on this page; do not cite it for them.

name: Wikimedia EventStreams recentchange (incremental feed)
what: Server-sent-events stream of recent changes across Wikimedia wikis, including wikidatawiki; backed by Kafka; resumable from stream position.
why_it_matters: Lets the people+orgs graph keep T0 current between weekly dumps by replaying edits for Q5 and org-class items.
numbers: Endpoint stream.wikimedia.org/v2/stream/recentchange (per search result, not fetched). Pywikibot EventStreams example filters type=edit, wiki=wikidatawiki.
note: Endpoint string came from a search snippet; check on wikitech before relying on it. The stream carries edits, not full entity JSON.

name: QLever SPARQL endpoint for Wikidata
what: Public QLever SPARQL service over Wikidata, faster than WDQS for counting and large scans; needs explicit PREFIX declarations.
why_it_matters: Counts can be taken without a dump; good for sanity-checking T0 totals and for pulling subsets in pages.
numbers: Measured 2026-10-14: COUNT of ?x wdt:P31 wd:Q5 = 13,738,078 humans. COUNT DISTINCT of ?x wdt:P31/wdt:P279* wd:Q43229 = 4,986,530 organisation-class items. Same query on query.wikidata.org (WDQS) returned 4,986,579 for the org count; WDQS timed out on the human count.
note: Counts differ by about 50 between QLever and WDQS, consistent with a different snapshot time. Full-text index claim was NOT verified.

name: DBpedia ontology and live SPARQL endpoint

numbers: Ontology page (undated, fetched 2026-10-14): Person 1,592,912; Organisation 317,867. Live endpoint measured 2026-10-14: COUNT DISTINCT ?x a dbo:Person with an English rdfs:label = 1,277,612 (a plain COUNT without the label filter returned 5,056,927, which likely mixes graphs; do not use it).

name: Pantheon data downloads (2.0 person files and 1.0 legacy)

Site text says it has data on more than 85,000 biographies, which conflicts with 126k rows.
ui_notes: Columns include id, wd_id, wp_id, slug, name, occupation, prob_ratio, gender, twitter, alive, l, hpi_raw, birthplace/deathplace with lat/lon and geonameid, birthyear, deathyear. Use wd_id as the join key to Wikidata.

name: Pantheon 1.0: a manually verified dataset of globally famous biographies (Yu et al., 2016)
what: Paper describing the Pantheon 1.0 dataset and the Historical Popularity Index (HPI). Published in Scientific Data 2:150075, doi 10.1038/sdata.2015.75.
why_it_matters: Defines how HPI is built (languages, pageviews, age); needed to explain any popularity score in the graph.
numbers: 11,341 biographies with more than 25 Wikipedia language editions; pageviews 2008-2013 (Yu et al., per search snippets, 2016). Paper licence CC BY 4.0 (arXiv PDF text, fetched by search 2026-10-14).
note: The exact HPI Equation 4 with weights was NOT retrieved (PDF fetch exceeded size limit; Nature page redirected to login). Approximation in the 2025 GDP paper (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2505.09399): log10(V) + ln(L) + log4(A), minus (70-A)/7 when A<70; R^2=0.76 against Pantheon HPI. Treat as approximation only.

name: GLEIF LEI records and Golden Copy
what: Legal-entity identifier database with Level 1 (who is who), Level 2 (parent relationships) and reporting exceptions, published as Golden Copy files.
why_it_matters: Authoritative legal-entity list for companies and funds worldwide; the best free org-entity spine with parent links.
numbers: GLEIF LEI API api.gleif.org/api/v1/lei-records total = 3,460,635 (measured 2026-10-14). Golden Copy issued three sets of files daily (GLEIF download page). Q2 2026 business report: 87.9% of the LEI population fully corroborated Level 1 data (https://www.gleif.org/lei-data/global-lei-index/download-global-lei-system-business-reports/download-global-lei-system-business-report-q2-2026/q2-2026-quarterly_business_report.pdf).

note: borrow-idea: interview-to-agent pattern for the advisor; last push Nov 2024; the 1,000-person bank is restricted, not in the repo.

note: use: diarization turns for attribution; code is MIT but pretrained pipelines are gated on Hugging Face and carry their own model licences (not checked here).

name: MahmoudAshraf97/whisper-diarization

name: modelscope/3D-Speaker

note: borrow-idea: strong embeddings for voiceprint attribution; Apache-2.0; last push Dec 2025; sherpa-onnx covers the same need in one dependency.

name: modelscope/FunASR

ui_notes: Active-learning pair review is the model for the yes/no/unsure queue that Haiku checkers can clear.
note: borrow-idea: take the active-learning pair-review loop; Splink does the matching; no need to run dedupe itself.

name: cosmos.gl (@cosmos.gl/graph)
what: GPU WebGL force-graph engine; layout and drawing run in shaders, so the CPU is not the bottleneck. Engine behind Cosmograph. Hover, click, right-click/long-press, pinch zoom, fitView, point-clustering force (v2), collision force (v3).
why_it_matters: Only open-source option found that claims to draw the full 339k-node / ~900k-edge person-work graph interactively without a server-side layout. Best candidate for an overview of the whole graph where an ego view is not enough.
numbers: README: 'hundreds of thousands of points and links on modern hardware' (github.com/cosmosgl/graph). 1.3k stars, 86 forks (same page). OpenJS blog claims over one million nodes and links (https://openjsf.org/blog/introducing-cosmos-gl), vendor claim, untested. iOS/Android WebGL extension gaps noted in search summary.
ui_notes: Steal the clustering force: setPointClusters / setPointClusterStrength pulls people sharing a topic into visible groups without pre-computed layouts. Hover highlights the topmost overlapping point and skips GPU work when the mouse is still.
note: MIT (repo LICENCE file and README, fetched 2026-10-14). | check: gh api cosmosgl/graph: 1,296 stars, 86 forks, MIT (row 1.3k / 86 forks, correct).

name: Cosmograph
what: Browser network and embedding explorer built on cosmos.gl, with DuckDB-Wasm for in-browser filter and aggregate and Mosaic for pre-aggregated cached updates. Intended for exploring networks and AI embeddings.
why_it_matters: Shows the architecture we would want: keep the data in an in-browser columnar store, aggregate on filter, and push only the visible subset to the GPU renderer.
numbers: Docs: GPU layouts for 'hundreds of thousands or millions of nodes and links' in seconds (vendor claim). Docs also say most CPU force layouts 'hit performance walls around 50,000 nodes' (cosmograph.app/docs-general/concept/). No hard limit stated.
ui_notes: Filter + histogram + timeline panels drive a GPU graph; selection in one panel filters the others. Pattern worth copying: aggregate in DuckDB/Mosaic, render only the filtered subset.
note: LICENCE CONFLICT, unresolved. Search summary says @cosmograph/cosmos is CC-BY-NC-4.0 (non-commercial, contact maintainers for commercial use); the concept page does not state a licence and its Citing and licensing page was not fetched. Do not ship @cosmograph/* without confirming. The cosmos.gl engine underneath is MIT.

name: graphology
what: Graph data model for JS/TS (directed, undirected, mixed, multi). Event emitter used as sigma.js backend. Standard library with layouts (ForceAtlas2 etc.), traversals, generators and a metrics package (density, etc.). Community detection is a separate package (graphology-communities-louvain).
why_it_matters: The data layer for a browser explorer: load the 900k person-work edges once, compute degree, neighbourhoods and Louvain communities in a worker, and feed sigma. Also lets us prototype clustering off the server.
numbers: 1.8k stars (github.com/graphology/graphology). No published node-count benchmark on the repo page; treat 339k nodes as untested and benchmark ourselves.
ui_notes: Use graph events (nodeAdded, edgeAdded) to drive incremental expansion: each click adds neighbours to the same graph instead of reloading.
note: MIT (LICENSE.txt, fetched 2026-10-14). | check: gh api graphology/graphology: 1,760 stars, 117 forks, MIT (row 1.8k, correct).

name: Gephi Lite
what: Browser version of Gephi. Runs with no server; data stays on the user's machine; optional save/load via GitHub Gists. Built on sigma.js and graphology. Open a GEXF file from a URL, embed in iFrame or drive with a JS driver. Lighter than desktop Gephi: smaller networks, fewer operations.
why_it_matters: Reference for a no-server exploration tool with layouts, filters and statistics in the browser. Also a link-out target: we can export GEXF and let power users open it.
numbers: 354 stars (github.com/gephi/gephi-lite). No published node limit found; the repo does not state one. Developers describe it as for 'smaller networks' (publicdatalab.org interview).
ui_notes: Left-panel filter and ranking stack (attribute filters, partition colouring, ranking size) with live preview. Good model for a people-graph filter sidebar.
note: GPL-3.0 (README and sidebar). Copyleft: reuse the idea or link out, do not copy code into a non-GPL repo. | check: gh api gephi/gephi-lite: 354 stars, 48 forks, licence GPL-3.0 (row 354 correct; licence not stated in row).

name: react-force-graph (2D, 3D, VR, AR)
what: React wrappers over force-graph (2D canvas), 3d-force-graph (ThreeJS/WebGL), VR (A-Frame) and AR (AR.js) with identical interfaces. Click, hover and drag handlers; autoPauseRedraw stops canvas redraw when layout settles.
why_it_matters: Fastest path to a working React explorer prototype for a few thousand nodes (ego view or a topic cluster). Not the right tool for 339k nodes in 2D canvas.
numbers: 3.3k stars (github.com/vasturiano/react-force-graph). No node-count limit stated. cooldownTime defaults to 15000 ms. enablePointerInteraction is 'at the cost of performance' (README).
ui_notes: autoPauseRedraw plus cooldownTime gives the settle-then-freeze feel; use it for ego views so the layout stops moving and the user can read labels.
note: MIT (README licence section, fetched 2026-10-14). | check: gh api vasturiano/react-force-graph: 3,324 stars, 357 forks, MIT (row 3.3k, correct).

name: Cytoscape.js
what: Graph theory library with an optional renderer for interactive graphs. Compound nodes, many layouts and an extensions ecosystem (70 listed). Tests in Mocha and Playwright; monthly feature releases.
why_it_matters: Mature option with compound (nested) nodes, which fit a person -> organisation or topic -> sub-topic hierarchy for collapsing clusters. Canvas-based, so good for thousands, not hundreds of thousands.
numbers: 11.2k stars, 1.7k forks (github.com/cytoscape/cytoscape.js). No large-graph figures on the repo page; benchmark script exists (npm run benchmark) with no published results.
ui_notes: Compound nodes: collapse a topic cluster into one parent node, expand on double-click. Same idea as cluster-to-supernode.
note: MIT (repo licence section, fetched 2026-10-14). | check: gh api cytoscape/cytoscape.js: 11,237 stars, 1,680 forks, MIT (row 11.2k / 1.7k, correct).

name: Kumu
what: Hosted relationship-mapping and stakeholder-map SaaS with a visual editor, views/filters and storytelling. Renders in WebGL (faster, less visual variety) or other modes.
why_it_matters: Benchmark for non-technical 'map' UX: named views, filter by element type, and story-mode walk-throughs. Not a fit for 339k nodes; no self-host for free tier.
numbers: Docs: no hard limit on elements, connections or maps; 'practical limit that will be different for each Kumu user'; animation and loading slow down with large imports (no figure given). Third-party FreeTier listing: $9/month and $20/month per project (unverified; check kumu.io/pricing).
ui_notes: Views as saved filter presets (show only some element types, hide the rest). Story mode steps through a curated sequence of nodes. Worth copying for curated 'stories' on the explore page.
note: Proprietary SaaS; free tier limits per the FreeTier listing, unverified.

name: Oligrapher (LittleSis)
what: JavaScript app for annotated network maps built from LittleSis data (who-knows-who in business and government). Click-through annotation series to tell a story; drag nodes and edges; force-directed or preset layouts; undo/redo; export SVG or JPEG; import from LittleSis and other APIs.
why_it_matters: Closest existing pattern to 'curated walk-through of a network': a person-centred story with annotated steps. Directly relevant to making the people graph readable for non-experts.
numbers: 112 stars, 1,438 commits (github.com/public-accountability/oligrapher). No node limit stated. Maps hosted on LittleSis.org (count not checked).
ui_notes: Story mode: each step is a view with a caption; click to advance. Export SVG for sharing. Map editing in-place (drag edges to re-link).
note: GPL-3.0 (repo page, fetched 2026-10-14). Copyleft; reuse the pattern, not the code. | check: gh api public-accountability/oligrapher: 112 stars, 22 forks, GPL-3.0; row 112 stars correct; 1,438 commits not checked.

name: Obsidian graph view (and Fast 3D Graph plugin)
what: Built-in global and local note graph. Local graph = depth-limited neighbourhood of the current note with filters (tags, folders, orphans). Switched SVG to canvas per staff reply. Community plugin Fast 3D Graph renders via WebGL.
why_it_matters: Shows the everyday pattern most people already know: local depth-1/2 graph around the current item, plus filters. The global graph failing at scale is the lesson: no one can browse a full hairball.
numbers: No official cap. Forum estimates: practical ceiling roughly 5k-25k notes depending on hardware; 35k-file vault black-screened for ~5 min; 130k-note vault froze (forum reports, not official). Fast 3D Graph plugin claims ~75 fps at 20,000 nodes and handles 50,000+ (community.obsidian.md/plugins/fast-graph).
ui_notes: Local graph with depth slider and filter by folder/tag. Orphan toggle hides isolated nodes to cut clutter. Steal the depth slider as the explicit expansion control.
note: Obsidian is proprietary; Fast 3D Graph plugin licence not checked.

name: Connected Papers
what: Builds one graph around an origin paper. Candidate pool is about 50,000 papers, of which only the few dozen most similar are shown. Similarity = co-citation plus bibliographic coupling. Force-directed layout. Click a node to highlight the shortest similarity path back to the origin. Also lists prior works (frequently cited foundations) and derivative works (papers citing many of the graph members).
why_it_matters: The clearest example of hairball avoidance by construction: show a small, meaningful subgraph (~tens of nodes) from a huge corpus, not the whole corpus. Directly maps to 'ego or similarity neighbourhood of one person, limited to top-k'.
numbers: ~50,000 candidates, few dozen shown (CASRAI guide https://casrai.org/guides/connected-papers, secondary source). Node size = citation count; colour = publication year. Exact similarity weighting not published.
ui_notes: Shortest-path-to-origin highlight on click; year colour ramp; separate lists for prior and derivative works. Copy: 'why is this person near that one' path highlight.
note: Proprietary; free tier and pricing not checked. The about page fetched with title only, so the mechanics rely on the secondary sources.

name: Litmaps
what: Literature map tool. Seed papers arranged on axes: x = publication year, y = citation count. Hollow nodes = suggested papers cited by the seeds. Seed maps and Discover maps (several seeds).
why_it_matters: A time-by-impact axis layout is an immediately readable 2D plot that scales to many nodes without a force layout. Good model for a people-by-year-by-work-count view.
numbers: 270M+ paper catalogue (per litmaps.com, vendor claim, via comparison page). Seed limit disputed across sources: one review says 1 seed on Seed map, 20 seeds on free Discover map. Pro tier pricing listed differently by two 2026/older sources; unverified.
ui_notes: X/Y axis encoding with hollow vs solid node styling for suggested vs known. Copy hollow-node idea to separate 'known' work from 'suggested' connections.
note: Proprietary SaaS; pricing unverified.

name: ResearchRabbit
what: Collections-based discovery tool. Start from seed papers and get recommendations for similar, earlier and later works, built from co-authors, related works and citations. Collections are ongoing and updated. Authors can appear as two nodes in collaboration views.
why_it_matters: The 'seed set -> expand by relation type' pattern: each recommendation is labelled by why it appeared (earlier, later, similar, co-author). Matches how a user would browse people via shared works.
numbers: 310M+ papers per researchrabbit.ai (vendor claim, via comparison page). Free per one review; unverified.
ui_notes: Relation-typed expansion (earlier / later / similar / co-author) as separate tabs. Copy: label every expansion by its edge type.
note: Proprietary, free to use per one review (unverified).

name: Inciteful
what: Free online citation-network explorer that builds user-defined graphs from OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar and Crossref. Seed-based expansion of a citation neighbourhood.
why_it_matters: A free, public example of the same expansion model over an open scholarly graph, relevant if we ever want to layer OpenAlex metadata on top of our people graph.
numbers: No node limit found. Official GitHub repo not located in search, so licence and code availability unknown.
ui_notes: Seed-set graph with a stated data source per edge (OpenAlex, S2, Crossref). Copy: show provenance on each edge.
note: Licence unknown; repo not found in this search.

name: Nomic Atlas
what: Hosted embedding map. Layout via UMAP below 50k points and the Nomic Project optimiser at 50k+ points (Python docs default). Metadata filter, regex and semantic lasso selection; user-supplied 2D coordinates accepted.
why_it_matters: Proof of the 2D-map-at-scale pattern for a hosted product; shows the 50k threshold where layout method switches. Useful as a reference UI, not as a dependency (proprietary, hosted).
numbers: Release notes: selections work at the 'tens of millions' scale (vendor claim, docs.nomic.ai/atlas/release-notes). Layout threshold: UMAP < 50,000 points, Nomic Project >= 50,000 (Python docs).
ui_notes: Lasso plus regex plus metadata filter in one bar. Accepting user-supplied x/y lets us push our own precomputed person coordinates.
note: Proprietary hosted service; pricing not checked.

name: deck.gl (visgl)
what: WebGL2/WebGPU layer framework from vis.gl. ScatterplotLayer for point maps; aggregation layers (hexbin, grid) for very dense point sets. Instancing gives millions of points in one draw.
why_it_matters: Right tool for the overview layer of 339k people as points with aggregation at low zoom. Pairs with a sigma ego view. Avoids edge rendering by design.
numbers: Google Maps codelab: 'hundreds of thousands' easily, 'millions' when optimised. Uber blog: 860K circles instanced (https://www.uber.com/blog/visualizing-data-sets-deck-gl-framework/). Property-assessment blog warns aggregation beats scatter at high density.
ui_notes: Aggregate at low zoom (hexbin counts), switch to individual points on zoom-in. Copy the zoom-driven level of detail.
note: Licence NOT verified from a fetched page; the search returned none. From memory it is MIT, but check github.com/visgl/deck.gl LICENSE before use. The URL given is a secondary guide.

name: Graphistry (PyGraphistry + GPU server)
what: Dataframe-native Python graph visual analytics. WebGL client renders graphs in the browser; server-side GPU analytics (RAPIDS) for larger graphs. GFQL query language with a subset of Cypher, optional GPU acceleration. Optional graph autoML (UMAP, feature engineering, GNN support).
why_it_matters: Reference for 'big graph in a browser, heavy lifting on a GPU box' split. We could keep the 339k graph on the server and stream a filtered subgraph to a WebGL client.
numbers: 2.6k stars, BSD-3-Clause (github.com/graphistry/pygraphistry). Client: up to 8MM nodes + edges at once; older client GPUs smooth at 100K-2MM elements (PyPI listing, https://pypi.org/project/graphistry/0.34.14). GPU mode '100X+ speedups' (repo). Demo 80,000+ Facebook friendships.
ui_notes: Server-side filter then client-side render; the split keeps the browser light. Copy the 'filter on server, draw subset' loop.
note: PyGraphistry BSD-3-Clause (repo sidebar). Server licence NOT stated on the page; check before self-hosting. | check: gh api graphistry/pygraphistry: 2,569 stars, BSD-3-Clause (row 2.6k, BSD-3, correct).

name: OCCRP Aleph (network diagrams and timelines)
what: Investigative data platform. Explore entities visually through network diagrams and timelines. Lets users pivot from an entity to its connections across datasets.
why_it_matters: Shows a people-plus-documents graph explored through entity pages with a timeline and a network pane side by side. Relevant to people -> works browsing.
numbers: No node-count limit found. MIT licence per IADB catalogue (https://knowledge.iadb.org/en/code-development/open-source-solutions/occrp-aleph). Aleph Pro rebuild announced (OCCRP), licence not verified. One aggregator marks one repo as dormant (unverified).
ui_notes: Entity page with linked network and timeline tabs; pivot by clicking an entity. Copy: an entity page is the unit of navigation, not the whole graph.
note: MIT per IADB catalogue and OpenAleph FAQ (secondary). Aleph Pro licence unverified.

name: Pantheon (MIT Media Lab Macro Connections, built by Datawheel)
what: Public site browsing notable people by country, city, occupation and era. Lists for People, Places and Occupations; profile pages for each; a Born on This Day feed; download and API pages; Trending profiles from Wikipedia pageviews.
why_it_matters: Browsing people by facets (occupation, country, era) instead of a graph is the browsable default for 339k people. Pantheon's facet pages are the model for our people index; the graph sits behind each profile.
numbers: Site claims data on more than 85,000 biographies (pantheon.world). Our graph: 339,217 people. Pantheon's dataset is the curated subset, not comparable on scale.
ui_notes: Facet listing pages (occupation x country combinations, eras) as entry points; profile page shows related people. Copy the occupation x country combination pages as landing pages for slices of the graph.
note: Footer links Creative Commons BY-SA 4.0 for the site content (per fetched page). Data licence and code not checked. | check: pantheon.world homepage: '85,000+ Biographies' (row 85,000, correct).

name: Histomania
what: Timeline browser for comparing events and people across history, sourced from Wikidata.
why_it_matters: Timeline as the main axis for people in time, with comparison across individuals. Matches the year dimension in our person-work edges.
numbers: No node count found. Listed on the Wikidata visualisation tools page (https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Wikidata:Tools/Visualize_data).
ui_notes: Horizontal life-span bars per person on a shared time axis. Copy: a life-span lane view for a selected set of people.
note: Licence not checked; site-level tool.

name: Histropedia
what: Auto-generated interactive timelines built from Wikipedia and Wikidata, including a Wikidata Query Timeline app (SPARQL-driven) at js.histropedia.com.
why_it_matters: Shows that a timeline can be generated from a query, not hand-built, which we can do from our own edges (filter -> timeline).
numbers: No node count found. Listed on https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Wikidata:Tools/Visualize_data. Query Timeline app at https://js.histropedia.com/apps/query-timeline/.
ui_notes: Query -> timeline with category colouring and zoomable axis. Copy: the timeline is a view of the current filter, not a separate page.
note: Licence not checked.

name: Scholia
what: Wikidata front end for scholarly metadata. Publication lists per author, venue or organisation; citation bar charts; co-author graphs; topic pages built from SPARQL queries.
why_it_matters: Closest existing public example of a people-and-works graph browser: each person page has a co-author graph and a publication list. Good model for profile pages with a small ego graph.
numbers: No published node limit found. Uses Wikidata Query Service (per search summary). Listed in the Wikidata tools table (https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Wikidata:Tools/Visualize_data).
ui_notes: Person profile = list of works plus small co-author graph; topic page = chart set. Copy the profile-first layout: graph is secondary to a list.
note: Licence not verified (GitHub URL returned 404 on fetch); assumed open source, check before reuse.

name: Wikidata visualisation tools directory (SQID, Reasonator, Graphpedia, Wikidata Graph Builder, metaphacts, and others)
what: Community list of 61 Wikidata visualisation tools. Relevant entries: SQID (browse and query with property and class usage stats), Reasonator (enhanced item display), Graphpedia (explorable knowledge graphs of properties), Wikidata Graph Builder (d3 item graph), Wikidata metaphacts (entity explorer with pathfinding between items), GeneaWiki and Wikidata Descent Map (family trees filterable by date).

name: Wikidata (humans, P31=Q5)
what: Open multilingual knowledge graph. A person is an item with P31 (instance of) = Q5 (human), identified by a Q-id. Cross-identity is done with external-id properties (VIAF, ORCID, ISNI, MusicBrainz, IMDb and others). Identity resolution is community-curated: editors create items, merge duplicates by hand, and bulk-match external catalogues through Mix'n'match with human confirmation.
why_it_matters: The largest free, human-curated identity hub for people and the usual crosswalk backbone. We should link into it and copy its external-id pattern rather than rebuild it.
numbers: Total items 123,624,278 and humans 13,656,532 (11.8%, shown in an older table whose total is 115,913,183). Source: https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Wikidata:Statistics (page cites a 2026-08-29 data module but gives no date for the total). A UMBC handout reports about 10.3M humans using subclass traversal (undated, third-party).
ui_notes: Public SPARQL endpoint at query.wikidata.org for COUNT over P31/Q5. Not opened in this run.

Human count from the page's older table, so treat as a floor. | check: Wikidata:Statistics shows humans 13,656,532 but under a heading marked outdated (with total 115,913,183); current total is 123,624,278 items. Humans figure is in the page but its currency is unconfirmed; 11.8% share is against the old total (about 11.1% of current).

name: OpenAlex authors (disambiguated author entities)
what: Open scholarly index. Authors are ML clusters of authorship records. The match uses six signals: name similarity, co-author patterns, institutional affiliations (parsed from raw affiliation strings), research topics, citation patterns (self-citation and reference overlap), and ORCID when present. ORCID is treated as authoritative but is rare and not applied retroactively. IDs are A+number; post-July-2023 IDs have numbers above 5000000000. A9999999999 is the NULL author for authorships never disambiguated. Errors are fixed through curations and per-profile corrections. No public confidence score. Code and models are open source.
why_it_matters: The clearest public description of a production author-resolution pipeline with named features and an explicit handling of unresolved records. Its NULL-author bucket is a model for how to store the unresolved remainder.
numbers: 124,697,641 authors and 323,964,135 works, measured 9 Aug 2026 (third-party blog, not OpenAlex): https://jwatte.com/blog/openalex-open-index-of-research.md . Accuracy: arXiv 2502.11610 benchmarks OpenAlex vs Clarivate Scholar ID on 100 scholars per group; headline precision/recall not pulled.
ui_notes: API rate limits per the official help page (updated 12 Oct 2026): no key 10 req/s; free key or prepaid 30 req/s; annual plan 50 req/s; 429 on overrun. A key is recommended for larger use. Third-party sources say metered pricing began Feb 2026; not checked against OpenAlex pricing page.
note: Author count is from a third-party blog. Licence (CC0) not confirmed on fetched pages. | check: Live api.openalex.org/authors meta.count on 2026-10-14 is 96,474,526, not 124,697,641 (about 23% lower). Cited figure came from a third-party blog; replace with the API number.

name: ORCID registry
what: Self-asserted persistent researcher identifier (16-digit iD). Identity is claimed by the person, not inferred by a merge model. Other graphs (OpenAlex, Crossref, Scopus links) ingest ORCID as the authoritative key when it exists. The design point: user-asserted identity as ground truth, machine resolution only for the rest.
why_it_matters: The opposite design to ML clustering and the strongest identity key for researchers. Our graph should take an ORCID as a hard join key and never merge two different ORCIDs.
numbers: Official total not captured: the ORCID statistics page did not render figures in our fetch. Secondary (CASRAI, citing ORCID 2025 Year in Review): 10.5M active users at end-2025 and more than 1,500 member organisations in 69 countries: https://casrai.org/news/persistent-identifiers-2026-orcid-ror-raid-doi . The same CASRAI source also cites a conflicting 21M registered-iD claim.
ui_notes: Public website text is CC0 (per info.orcid.org). Public Data File Use Policy and Public API Terms are linked but their text was not retrieved.
note: Counts unverified; do not quote a total until the statistics page renders or the data file is checked.

Licence is proprietary with a free account.
why_it_matters: The largest people database we found. It is three orders of magnitude over the 1M falsifier and it shows what happens to identity at scale without strong merge: duplicates stay. A warning for our merge design.
numbers: 1.96 billion people and 4.27 billion sources in the Family Tree, updated 6 Oct 2026 per the FamilySearch company facts page (https://familysearch.org/en/newsroom/company-facts). Duplicate caveat: https://community.familysearch.org/en/discussion/94906/determining-number-of-persons-on-my-family-tree
ui_notes: Not inspected. FamilySearch has a developer API (not verified in this run).

name: OpenSanctions (persons, PEPs and sanctions)
what: Compiled graph of sanctions, PEP and regulatory entities from 470+ sources, modelled in FollowTheMoney. Entities are linked to relatives, associates and companies. Matching runs in the open-source yente API, which is the same API in the on-prem deployment. The matcher uses identifiers to separate true matches from false positives. Free data is CC BY-NC 4.0. Commercial use needs a licence: in-house screening licence (flat rate), reseller/OEM licence, or hosted Screening API billed per query with prepaid credit bundles. Journalists, academics and public-interest bodies may qualify for free API access.
why_it_matters: A public-data people graph with an open matching engine and a documented data model. It is the most directly copyable identity-resolution design we found for people, and it is a falsifier hit: over 1M persons, not on the held list.
numbers: People 1,141,784; organisations 297,539; securities 274,623; crypto addresses 14,107; vessels and aircraft 10,555; enforcement notices 3,485; 47mn+ facts; 470+ sources. Source: https://www.opensanctions.org/licensing/ (no date shown). Bulk licence price is quote-only on the current page; a 2022 article gave EUR 595/month for bulk, dated: https://www.opensanctions.org/articles/2022-10-04-saas-api.md
ui_notes: Screening API billed by query with prepaid credits and free sign-up credits; per-call price not stated on the current page.

name: VIAF (Virtual International Authority File)
what: Union of national library authority files (over 50 contributors, including ISNI) into clusters, one per entity, each with a persistent numeric ID. Clusters are recomputed monthly, so IDs can merge or split. Records match on explicit identifiers, string matching, or both. Names with initials are no longer matched directly to full names after false merges. The ISNI quality team uses marker fields on corrected records to block false merges and to split clusters. Open data under ODC-BY.
why_it_matters: A mature multi-source person-merge pipeline that uses corrective marker fields and monthly re-clustering. Copy the split-marker idea and the conservative string-match rule.
numbers: Cluster and identifier counts not retrieved; the only figure found was the 2011 OCLC announcement (https://www.oclc.org/developer/news/2011/viaf-gets-bigger-and-better.en.html). Check viaf.org for current totals.
ui_notes: ISNI records carry status: assigned, provisional or suspect.
note: Guidelines PDF seen in search results and not read in full. Totals missing.

name: Scopus Author Profiles (Elsevier)
what: Author profile graph built from indexed works. Profiles are created automatically and split when an author's name, subject area, affiliation or co-authors change, so one person can have several profiles. Merges and splits are requested through the Author Feedback Wizard and reviewed by Elsevier before being applied. University guidance puts review at 1 to 2 weeks. Advice: verify by document titles and co-authors, not name similarity.
why_it_matters: A conservative-split, human-merge design. It shows the cost of splitting by default: a long review queue for users. Our queue should accept merges as well as splits.
numbers: Profile total not found. Review timelines from university guidance (third-party, approximate).
ui_notes: Feedback wizard can merge, split, remove documents and correct details.
note: Process described from secondary guides; the Elsevier page was not fully read. Count missing.

name: UK Companies House officers register

Licence is described as Open Government Licence v3.0 by one secondary source; a forum answer cites the CDPA s.47 database right.
why_it_matters: A legally filed, government-issued people-to-company link. It is the best source for linking a person to the companies they run, and it is free at the point of use.
numbers: Rate limit 600 requests per 5 minutes per key (secondary source, Companies House API docs). Officer total not found.
