name: Wikidata data model (statements, qualifiers, references, ranks)
what: Official spec of Wikidata's model: items and properties, statements with qualifiers and references, three ranks (preferred, normal, deprecated), unknown and no-value markers.
why_it_matters: The only open all-domain graph that already carries per-claim sources and rank-based conflict handling at scale; the template to copy or beat for people and orgs.
numbers: ~123.6M content pages and 2.56B page edits per Special:Statistics (captured undated); ~13,972 properties, ~76% external identifiers (data model page); ~68% of statements referenced (2021 paper, secondary).
ui_notes: Statement cards show value, qualifiers and references; ranks are not visually distinguished in the web UI (open Phabricator task, secondary source).
note: item > statement(property, value, qualifiers, references, rank); no statement-level truth flag, ranks instead | check: Wikidata Data_model and Statistics pages: 13,972 properties, 76% external identifiers, 123,624,278 items, 2,556,092,845 edits (all match). The 68% referenced statement share was not checked.

name: Wikidata at query scale (WDQS, QLever mirror, graph split)
what: How Wikidata is queried at scale: Blazegraph WDQS being replaced by QLever candidate; scholarly items split into a second query service on 9 May 2025; weekly RDF dumps.
why_it_matters: Shows the practical ceiling of one monolithic RDF store and the fix (split subgraphs plus a faster engine), which we would need for an all-of-history people+org graph.
numbers: ~17B triples (2022 workshop paper); 20B triples in QLever's full-Wikidata benchmark; ~1B triples/year growth (Wikidata team, 2023); WikiCite data >50% of triples (2025 CEUR paper).
ui_notes: Public QLever endpoint lags the live site by up to a week because it loads weekly dumps.
note: RDF triples in Blazegraph/QLever; split by subgraph (scholarly vs rest)

name: Factoid prosopography model (KCL, Bradley, Byzantine tradition)
what: Prosopography modelled as a collection of source-level assertions (factoids): each factoid is a spot in a source saying something about a person, linked to sources, persons, places, possessions and classification schemes.
why_it_matters: Direct ancestor of claim-level people graphs; keeps conflicting sources side by side instead of forcing one biography per person, which is the exact behaviour a 'every human ever' graph needs.
numbers: Tens of thousands of factoids per project (KCL page); Prosopography of the Byzantine World core ~60,000 factoids, ~7,500 seals (older Oxford DH page).
ui_notes: Users assemble their own narrative from assertions; no per-person article is authored.
note: factoid = source + assertion about person(s); FPO is an OWL/RDFS ontology on GitHub

name: SNAP:DRGN (Standards for Networking Ancient Prosopographies)
what: KCL-based pilot that defines minimal RDF standards for person data in ancient prosopographies and gives each identified person a URI so name references across datasets link to one person, Pelagios-style.
why_it_matters: Concrete crosswalk-ID pattern: many prosopographies (PIR, LGPN, Trismegistos, Papyri.info) share URIs for the same person rather than merging records.
numbers: Not stated on the intro page; PIR persons in PIR2 A-R and PIR1 S-Z carry SNAP IDs (open-epihub and Digital Classicist pages).
ui_notes: Scholarly, no end-user UI; API-level linking.
note: person URI per identified person; minimal RDF person core; crosswalk by URI

name: Trismegistos People (TM People)
what: Papyrological person database for non-royal individuals in Egypt 800 BC to AD 800, with separate PER (person) and REF (attestation) tables that link persons to the documents that mention them.
why_it_matters: Clean two-table model of person vs. attestation, with IDs that cross-reference many other ancient-person databases; a working example of a merged-but-linked identity layer.
numbers: 380,676 person records and 555,414 attestations (about-page snippet; an older ISAW index gives 458,045 attestations); fetch of the page failed on certificate, so counts are from search snippet.
ui_notes: Search by name, place, date; each person has a TM ID and per-attestation document links.
note: PER table (person) + REF table (attestation to document); TM IDs crosswalk to other DBs

name: Prosopography of the Byzantine World (PBW, KCL)
what: Byzantine prosopography built from factoids (one assertion per source mention), restructured mid-1990s from print articles into a data-first resource; covers AD 1025-1180 in its current scope.
why_it_matters: Proof that a factoid-first database can run for decades and be re-used; a template for the source-first design of a people+orgs graph.
numbers: Core ~60,000 factoids, 2,774 narrative units, ~7,500 seals (older Oxford DH description); current person total not found.
ui_notes: Browse by person page assembled from factoids; each factoid cites its source.
note: factoid rows (source, person, place, possession) plus classification schemes

name: Prosopographia Imperii Romani (PIR) online and data repo
what: Print prosopography of Roman elite (1st-3rd century) with an online name index and API; PIR2 A-R and PIR1 S-Z carry unique IDs; a GitHub data repo is listed under CC BY 4.0.
why_it_matters: Shows the limit of a print-first prosopography: biographical content withheld for publisher reasons, only names and citations open. Good lesson on licensing the data layer separately from the text.
numbers: Scope of Roman elite for 300 years; record count not confirmed in this slice.
ui_notes: Name search returns names and bibliographic citations; full biographies are not public.
note: name + bibliographic citation per person; SNAP IDs; partial JSON API

name: VIAF (Virtual International Authority File)
what: OCLC-run cluster service that matches national authority files (LC, GND, BnF and others) and merges their records into a super-cluster per person or organisation, without replacing the source records.
why_it_matters: The largest working example of a crosswalk-first identity layer for people and corporate bodies: source IDs stay, a derived cluster ID sits on top, and the crosswalk is rebuilt on a schedule.
numbers: Cluster run monthly; many national agencies contribute (count not confirmed in this slice); LC-GND-OCLC proof of concept 2003, BnF joined 2007.
ui_notes: Public cluster page per VIAF ID with source-record links and name variants.
note: source record IDs crosswalk to derived cluster ID; monthly re-cluster can split or merge IDs

name: FamilySearch Family Tree (one shared world tree)
what: Single shared genealogy tree in which each person is one profile; duplicates are merged person-by-person with field-level choice, possible-duplicate hints, safeguards and an Undo Merge after each merge.
why_it_matters: The largest single tree of people with live merge practice; its merge rules (block living/deceased, different sex, parent-child) and change-log reasons are directly reusable for a people graph.
numbers: ~1.74 billion names as of July 2025 (FamilySearch); no official duplicate count found.
ui_notes: Merge page shows recommendation levels (no obvious problems, potential, not recommended, unable to merge), Not a Match marking, and reason statement required.
note: one profile per person; merge = survivor + field picks + change log; Undo Merge | check: FamilySearch blog: about 1.74 billion names as of July 2025; matches row.

name: WikiTree (one profile per person, trusted-list merges)
what: Open genealogy wiki with one profile per person; duplicate profiles are merged only when both owners agree, and the merge is irreversible once completed.
why_it_matters: Shows the governance cost of merges: owner consent plus irreversibility keeps data clean but slows throughput; contrast with reversible judgement-graph merges.
numbers: Count not checked in this slice.
ui_notes: Merge flow asks owners to agree, then lets the editor pick which field values to keep.
note: one profile per person; consent-gated, irreversible merge

name: Geni World Family Tree (matching and merge centre)
what: Commercial genealogy site aiming for one World Family Tree; duplicate matching across user trees plus MyHeritage smart and record matching; merges need profile owners' approval.
why_it_matters: Demonstrates a matching pipeline fed by multiple trees and records; the merge bottleneck is owner response, not matching accuracy.
numbers: Count not confirmed in this slice; blog-era (2015) reports only.
ui_notes: Merge Center lists suggested matches; users must add enough generations for matching to fire.
note: per-user trees merged into a world tree via matching + owner approval

name: OpenCorporates (statement model for companies and officers)
what: Largest open company registry aggregator across ~140 jurisdictions; the API reference says the data moved from a per-item datum model to a statement model with finer provenance, with existing datums migrated to statements.
why_it_matters: Live example of an org graph that switched to per-fact provenance mid-life; the migration is the thing to learn from, not just the scale.
numbers: 220M+ companies and 310M+ officers (OpenCorporates knowledge base); 143M companies and 128 jurisdictions in 2018 blog post.
ui_notes: Company page with jurisdiction code, officers, filings; open-data licence for non-commercial use.
note: company + officer + jurisdiction; datum migrated to statement with source

name: ROR (Research Organization Registry) data dumps on Zenodo
what: Open registry of research organisations with stable ROR IDs, released as versioned JSON (schema v1 and v2) and CSV dumps; the JSON is the format of record.
why_it_matters: A small, curated, versioned org registry with a stable ID and a published schema switch, good for the org axis of the graph; it is organisations only, no people.
numbers: 120,196 organisations in v1.74 (24 Nov 2025); 119,173 in v1.72; the Zenodo record URL was matched to a release in search snippets, not verified.
ui_notes: Searchable registry on ror.org; API default moved to v2 July 2025 and v1 deprecated Dec 2025.
note: org record with stable ID, versioned JSON dump, schema v2 switch

name: CIDOC-CRM actor model (E39 Actor, E21 Person, E74 Group, E82 Actor Appellation)
what: ISO standard event-centric cultural-heritage ontology: people and groups are actors, names are appellations attached to actors, and life facts (birth, death, formation) are events rather than attributes.
why_it_matters: The standard vocabulary for a person as an actor with event-based life history and appellation-based names; the event-not-attribute choice is the one to copy for dated facts about people and orgs.
numbers: Standard; no scale claim (not a dataset).
ui_notes: Ontology only; used in LINCS and museum graphs.
note: actor + appellation + event (birth, death, formation) with P-properties

name: Nanopublications (assertion + provenance + publication info, Trusty URIs)
what: Scholarly format where each claim is a named graph of three parts: the assertion, its provenance, and publication info, made immutable with a hash-based Trusty URI.
why_it_matters: The strongest published pattern for statement-level provenance and immutability; it is the closest thing to per-claim sourcing done as a standard, and it gives a way to cite a single claim.
numbers: Growing uptake across life sciences (DisGeNET published as nanopublications); no global count in these results.
ui_notes: Not a UI product; nanopub servers and a nanopub viewer exist.
note: named graph: assertion, provenance, pubinfo; Trusty URI for immutability

name: W3C PROV-O (provenance ontology)
what: W3C recommendation for provenance: Entity, Activity, Agent; wasGeneratedBy, wasDerivedFrom, wasAttributedTo, plus qualified influence classes.
why_it_matters: The standard vocabulary to reuse for who-said-what, but it has no native per-triple provenance; the page says a Bundle is the nearest tool, so statement-level sourcing must be built on top.
numbers: Standard; no scale claim.
ui_notes: Ontology only.
note: entity/activity/agent; bundles for named provenance sets; no triple-level provenance

name: Splink (probabilistic record linkage, Fellegi-Sunter)
what: Python library (UK Ministry of Justice) for probabilistic deduplication and linking of records without shared IDs, unsupervised EM training, blocking rules and clustering of match pairs into entity IDs.
why_it_matters: The most practical open tool for the entity-resolution step of a people+org graph at laptop scale; it runs on DuckDB and scales to Spark for 100M+ records.
numbers: ~1M records linked on a laptop in about a minute; 100M+ on Spark (project page); one user reports 30M addresses in under 5 hours on Databricks.
ui_notes: Interactive comparison and cluster charts in the docs.
note: pairwise match probability then clustered entity IDs; EM-trained m/u parameters | check: Splink docs: links a million records on a laptop in approximately one minute; DuckDB or Spark for 100+ million records; matches row.

name: nomenklatura (OpenSanctions entity resolution and statements framework)
what: Framework behind OpenSanctions: entities stored as statements (one value per property, with dataset and date), judgements stored as positive or negative pairs, canonical IDs minted per positive decision, merges computed at export from the judgement graph.
why_it_matters: The closest open design to what we need: source-level statements, reversible merges by changing judgements (not data), and a blocking-based candidate list; the basic OpenSanctions facts are already held, this row is for the merge and statement design.
numbers: 130,000 entities would mean ~17B pairwise comparisons; 34,600 manual decisions in 8 weeks (31,000 positive); ~300,000 implied negative pairs.
ui_notes: Analysts compare pairs side by side in a text tool and record same/different.
note: statement (prop, value, dataset, date) + judgement graph + canonical ID; merge is a view | check: OpenSanctions 2021 blog: 130,000 entities, ~17B pairwise comparisons (130k x 130k cross-product), 34,600 manual decisions, 31,000 positive, ~300,000 negative pairs; all quoted correctly.

name: YAGO 4.5 (Wikidata with schema.org upper taxonomy and SHACL)
what: Knowledge base derived from Wikidata that puts Wikidata classes under a schema.org-style upper taxonomy (Person, Organization, Event, Place, etc.) with SHACL constraints for cleaning and reasoning.
why_it_matters: Shows how to clean Wikidata's class soup into a typed person/org layer with logical constraints; directly relevant to typing a people+org graph.
numbers: 49M entities and 109M facts (official page); paper arXiv 2308.11884 (SIGIR 2024).
ui_notes: Downloads as Turtle and N-Triples with SHACL schema files.
note: Wikidata-derived; schema.org upper classes; SHACL disjointness; facts without per-claim rank

name: Freebase (Metaweb; retired 2016)
what: Open, graph-shaped knowledge base of topics, types and properties with user-editable types under folksonomy rules; Google bought Metaweb in 2010 and announced the shutdown in Dec 2014, closing 2 May 2016 with Wikidata as the successor.
why_it_matters: The closest historical attempt at a community-curated all-of-world graph; its death is the cautionary case in the lessons section of the notes.
numbers: ~44M topics and 2.4B facts (January 2014, Wikipedia citing the Freebase page).
ui_notes: Freebase UI had topic pages and an MQL query explorer; closed with the API and widget.
note: topic + type + property graph (graphd, MQL); no per-fact sources; restricted schema edits

name: Google Knowledge Graph (last public scale figure, 2020)
what: Google's proprietary graph of entities and facts behind search panels; partly fed by Freebase and Wikipedia; no public implementation documentation.
why_it_matters: Shows the scale the commercial side reached, and that its inner data model is closed; it cannot be copied directly but sets the scale benchmark.
numbers: 500B facts about 5B entities (May 2020, Google); 570M entities and 18B facts at 2012 launch; third-party 2022 estimate 9.25B entities (unofficial).
ui_notes: Search knowledge panels and cards.
note: closed entity + fact graph; no public per-fact source model

name: Diffbot Knowledge Graph (people and organisations, auto-extracted)
what: Commercial knowledge graph built by automated extraction from the web, with person and organisation entities and facts; claims refreshes every few days and a changelog of enrichment.
why_it_matters: Proof that automated web extraction can produce a people+org graph at billions of entities; the open question is whether per-fact sources are exposed (vendor marketing only here).
numbers: April 2021 whitepaper: 1.3B+ person entities, 715M+ organisation entities, 242M+ articles; 2024 Workspace listing: 20B+ entities and 2T+ facts; refresh every 3-5 days (vendor claim).
ui_notes: API and Excel/Sheets add-ins; no open dump found.
note: entity + facts from web extraction; closed; no per-fact source exposed in these pages

name: OpenAlex author object (person profile as derived set of works)
what: Person-level profiles built by disambiguating name strings from works; the profile is a set of linked works, identity fields (ORCID, observed ORCIDs) and affiliations are derived from authorships, and fixes are made by changing the works.
why_it_matters: A clean derived-profile design: the person is a view over sourced works, so bad merges are fixed upstream; relevant for a people graph where facts come from documents.
numbers: Only ~1 in 10 profiles has a primary ORCID (page); counts and disambiguation method on linked pages not read.
ui_notes: API only; affiliations cover ~10 years, full history via works grouped by year.
note: person = derived view over works; ids (openalex, orcid, observed_orcids); updated_date stamp

name: Pantheon (MIT Media Lab) Historical Popularity Index
what: Ranking of 11,341 Wikipedia biographies present in more than 25 language editions, with verified birth date, birthplace, gender and a 3-level occupation taxonomy. Two popularity measures: L (number of language editions) and HPI, which combines L, time since birth and 2008-2013 pageviews.
why_it_matters: The closest existing people-ranking method with a published dataset and a stated formula family. It is our baseline to beat on bias; no validated alternative was found that beats it.
numbers: 11,341 biographies (MIT page, Jan 2016). HPI formula weights not published on the page. Earlier 2014 coverage cites a 15-edition threshold (sopitas.com) but the 2016 page says more than 25; treat as unresolved. Source: https://www.media.mit.edu/publications/pantheon-10-a-manually-verified-dataset-of-globally-famous-biographies/
ui_notes: Show L and HPI as separate columns with the component breakdown (languages, age, pageviews); show top-N per occupation and per country rather than one global list.
note: Biases: authors state English, Western, male and highly-educated editor bias plus recency bias; HPI uses pageviews so it skews to US and recent figures (Wikimedia Research Newsletter 2014). Pantheon 2.0 not found in search. | check: MIT Media Lab page: 11,341 biographies present in more than 25 language editions; published 5 Jan 2016. Matches.

name: Pantheon 1.0: a manually verified dataset of globally famous biographies (Yu, Ronen, Hu, Lu, Hidalgo)
what: Data paper behind Pantheon: the L and HPI measures, the occupation taxonomy, and a comparison with Murray's Human Accomplishments and with external accomplishment measures in tennis, swimming, car racing and chess.
why_it_matters: Only peer-style validation we found for a people-popularity index: popularity (L, HPI) correlates with individual accomplishment, read as a proxy for historical impact.
numbers: 11,341 biographies; more than 25 languages; pageviews 2008-2013. Correlation coefficients not shown on the MIT summary page; check the full paper. Source: https://www.media.mit.edu/publications/pantheon-10-a-manually-verified-dataset-of-globally-famous-biographies/
ui_notes: Cite the paper on the leaderboard footer; show the external-validation domains (tennis, chess) as a sanity panel.
note: Authors' own limitations: Wikipedia editors skew English, Western, male, educated, and recency-biased; the dataset is a view of multilingual Wikipedia as of May 2013.

name: Interactions of cultures and top people of Wikipedia from ranking of 24 language editions (Eom et al., PLoS ONE 2015)
what: Runs PageRank and 2DRank on the hyperlink graphs of 24 Wikipedia language editions and lists the top 100 historical figures per edition and per algorithm.
why_it_matters: A link-structure ranking of people that needs no pageview data; gives a per-language view that can be compared to pageview-based scores.
numbers: 24 language editions; top 100 per edition. Linnaeus ranks first under PageRank, Hitler first under 2DRank (Shortlist, https://shortlist.com/news/revealed-the-most-influential-people-ever). PLoS ONE 10(3): e0114825 (2015).
ui_notes: Show a per-edition toggle; show PageRank and 2DRank side by side because they disagree (Linnaeus vs. Hitler).
note: Biases: link structure rewards taxonomy and list articles (Linnaeus effect); 2DRank rewards outgoing-link density; per-language results differ sharply, so no single global order.

name: Who's Bigger? Where Historical Figures Really Rank (Skiena and Ward, 2013)
what: Book applying a PageRank-style score to the Wikipedia link graph to rank everyone with an article, with an explicit definition of significance as the social and cultural effect of an individual's achievement.
why_it_matters: The clearest public description of PageRank applied to people, and a good template for an explained composite; the reviews show how readers react to the output.
numbers: Top ranks reported in reviews: Jesus #1, Napoleon, Mohammed, Shakespeare in the top 4 (Big Think, https://develop.bigthink.com/?p=57344); Marie Antoinette 125th (SIAM News review as cited in search). Lowest-ranked example about #843,790 (review).
ui_notes: Show rank with the percentile and the rank of the same person under a second measure to expose disagreement.
note: Biases: link graph favours Western, English-heavy and historically canonical figures; reviewers question whether PageRank measures significance at all.

name: Cultural Anthropology through the Lens of Wikipedia: Historical Leader Networks, Gender Bias, and News-based Sentiment (arXiv 1508.00055)
what: Builds networks of historical leaders from Wikipedia and measures gender bias and news-based sentiment; uses Pantheon-style lists.
why_it_matters: Shows that a top-N built on Pantheon-type lists is dominated by Greek philosophers (top five: Aristotle, Plato, Jesus, Socrates, Alexander), which is the selection-bias evidence we need for our own cohort design.
numbers: Pantheon-derived list from 11,340 Wikipedia people pages; minimum 25 language editions; top five entries Aristotle, Plato, Jesus, Socrates, Alexander (per paper summary in search; verify in PDF).
ui_notes: Use as a warning panel: show how many of the top-N are from one region or era.
note: Biases: Murray Human Accomplishments source is textbook-based; leader networks inherit textbook canon.

name: Survival of the Notable: Gender Asymmetry in Wikipedia Collective Deliberations (Huq and Ciampaglia, arXiv 2411.04340; ACM HCI 2025)
what: Competing-risk survival analysis of Articles for Deletion discussions; tests how notability decisions differ for biographies of women versus men.
why_it_matters: Direct evidence that notability gatekeeping is gendered, so a ranking built on Wikipedia article existence inherits the gap before any scoring starts.
numbers: Women's biographies nominated for deletion sooner, but consensus takes longer; women's biographies more often merged into men's for historical figures (abstract, arXiv 2411.04340). Share of women biographies: 18.51% on English Wikipedia per the paper's citation of the Wikidata Human Gender Indicator.
ui_notes: Show gender share of the cohort next to every ranked list, with the cohort's expected share.
note: Bias: gender (article-level gatekeeping). Wikipedia's own page cites that 41% of AfD nominated biographies in April 2017 were about women when women were about 17% of biographies.

name: Women in Wikipedia are slightly more notable than men; gap larger for local heroes (EPJ Data Science)
what: Study of notability among biographies of women and men; finds the gender gap is larger for less-notable local figures than for superstars.
why_it_matters: A threshold-based notability cut (e.g. article exists) will admit men at lower notability and exclude women, so any rank with an existence filter needs a gender-stratified check.
numbers: Gap larger for local heroes than superstars (search summary of EPJ Data Science 2016 paper; check exact numbers in PDF).
ui_notes: Show a stratified view: rank within notability band so low-notability women are not hidden.
note: Bias: gender; glass-ceiling in inclusion barrier per authors.

name: We Need a Woman in Music: Exploring Wikipedia's Values on Article Priority (arXiv 2208.08426)
what: Studies which Wikipedia articles get priority (pageviews, editing); reports on biography gender in the top of the pageview ranking.
why_it_matters: Pageview-based fame ranks inherit editor priority; shows the bias is measurable in top-N lists.
numbers: 32% of biographies in the top 50,000 by pageviews are women; strong recency effect at the very top (search summary; verify in paper).
ui_notes: Show the gender share of the top-N against the cohort baseline on the page.
note: Bias: gender and recency; pageviews reward people in the news that year.

name: Global Gender Differences in Wikipedia Readership (Johnson et al., ICWSM)
what: Joins a global survey of 65,031 Wikipedia readers to reading logs; shows readership gender differences.
why_it_matters: Popularity rankings built on readership amplify existing imbalances unless they correct for reader gender; this is the evidence to cite for that claim.
numbers: 65,031 survey respondents plus reading logs (ICWSM abstract).
ui_notes: Caveat on pageview-based panels: say popularity reflects who reads, not only who matters.
note: Bias: gender of readers; popularity-based rankings can exacerbate imbalance.

name: QRank (Wikidata entity pageview score)
what: Weekly-published gzipped CSV ranking every Wikidata item by aggregated pageviews across Wikipedia and sister projects (Wikispecies, Wikibooks, Wikiquote and others).
why_it_matters: Joins to our people-graph by Wikidata ID; the cheapest current-popularity input we can actually get.
numbers: Score = aggregated pageviews across Wikimedia projects, no normalization described (Simon Willison, Apr 2024). Mirror SQLite DB 307MB (hikeratlas/qrank via same page).
ui_notes: Show the raw QRank and a log-scaled value; never show the raw view count as rank.
note: Biases: recency, English and US traffic, and bots/news spikes; no per-language split in the public file. | check: simonwillison.net 2024/Apr/21: QRank aggregates pageviews across Wikipedia, Wikispecies, Wikibooks, Wikiquote; gzipped CSV; mirror weekly; mirror SQLite DB 307MB. Matches.

name: Wikidata sitelink count as notability proxy
what: Count of Wikipedia language editions with an article for a Wikidata item (sitelinks). Long the default way to order Wikidata results.
why_it_matters: Cheap, cross-language breadth signal for all 339k people; available from the Wikidata dump with no pageview pipeline.
numbers: Sitelinks measure breadth across editions, not depth; the Phabricator discussion calls it not very accurate when a topic is mostly in one language (Wikimedia Phabricator; URL is a discussion task surfaced by search, content to verify).
ui_notes: Show as 'present in N editions'; use it as an input, not the headline score.
note: Bias: Western and English-heavy editions decide breadth; large-language-edition bias; sitelinks grow with age.

name: Semantic Scholar influential citations and h-index FAQ
what: Influential-citation flag from a machine-learning model using citation counts and citation context; h-index computed only from discoverable papers; the site advises against comparative use of h-index.
why_it_matters: A scholar-side impact input that already down-weights passing citations; usable for the works side of our ranking.
numbers: No single numeric threshold published in the FAQ text; flagging depends on full-text access (FAQ).
ui_notes: Show influential citations separately from total citations.
note: Biases: full-text access skews by publisher and field; h-index ignores career stage and field norms (Semantic Scholar's own warning).

name: OpenAlex author summary_stats (h-index, i10, cited_by_count)
what: Author records with cited_by_count, works_count and summary_stats (h-index, i10-index); the authors endpoint can sort by them.
why_it_matters: Free, open, and joinable to people by ORCID; the scholar-side works signal for our people graph.
numbers: Fields: cited_by_count, works_count, summary_stats.h_index, summary_stats.i10_index (OpenAlex author object docs). OpenAlex vs Scopus rank correlation is high in an arXiv study (arXiv 2404.17663), but author disambiguation was not checked.
ui_notes: Show h-index with works count and field; do not rank across fields on h-index alone.
note: Biases: field and career-length; author disambiguation errors; no method page for the author ranking itself was found.

name: Measuring academic influence: Not all citations are equal (arXiv 1501.06587)
what: Argues the h-index treats a highly cited and barely cited paper alike once they clear the threshold, and proposes weighting citations by influence, tested on ACL Fellows.
why_it_matters: Justifies weighting citations rather than counting them, the same logic as the Semantic Scholar influential flag.
numbers: Tested on ACL Fellows (search summary; check paper for correlation numbers).
ui_notes: If we show a works score, state that it is a weighted citation score, not an h-index.
note: Bias: field-dependent citation norms; h-index cannot compare across fields.

name: TIME 100 Most Influential People
what: Annual editor-curated list; nominations from alumni and international writing staff; separate Reader's Poll picks one winner.
why_it_matters: A human editorial gold-standard style list we can use as a validation set (who is on it, and in what year), not as a score.
numbers: No score; editors choose; Time's 2026 statement says there is no single metric for influence (KUTV coverage, https://kutv.com/news/entertainment/times-100-most-influential-people-of-2026-who-made-the-cut-noah-wyle-hilary-duff-alysa-liu-rhea-seehorn-victoria-beckham-hilary-knight-nikki-glaser).
ui_notes: Show as a badge (on Time 100 in year X) rather than a rank.
note: Biases: editor and alumni networks, US and media-facing people; no transparent method beyond the nomination process.

name: Forbes Celebrity 100 (earnings plus fame)
what: Ranks celebrities by earnings over a 12-month window plus a fame score built from Google hits, Blog Search, LexisNexis TV and radio mentions, Factiva press, magazine covers and social followers; a 2013 marketability score from E-Poll was added.
why_it_matters: The clearest mixed-signal commercial method: separates earnings from fame, and is a template for a fame-by-channel breakdown.
numbers: Earnings window June 2009 to June 2010 (2010 edition, Globe and Mail); fame counts 25 consumer magazines; 2013 marketability score 1-100 across 6,600 celebrities polled on 46 attributes (goodblacknews.org 2013).
ui_notes: Show the fame breakdown by channel, not one number; show a year stamp because the method has changed.
note: Biases: US-centric media sources (LexisNexis, US magazines), earnings favor film/TV, editorial opacity on the fame score. Forbes India 2026 article found in search is unreliable (illustrative table).

name: Klout (dead social influence score)
what: Social influence score 0-100 from cumulative online actions; bought by Lithium in 2014 and shut down on May 25, 2018.
why_it_matters: Evidence that a black-box influence score on platform activity does not survive; its failure is about opacity and platform dependence, not just algorithm quality.
numbers: Shut down 2018-05-25; Lithium reportedly paid about $200M in 2014 (Search Engine Journal and coverage; price is a secondary-source figure).
ui_notes: If we publish a score, publish the formula and the inputs; Klout's black-box score was the core complaint.
note: Reasons: parent said standalone service not aligned with long-term strategy; critics said the score method was never clear. Caution against platform-dependent inputs (Twitter/Facebook).

name: Kred Influence and Outreach scores
what: Social influence score on a 1-1000 scale with separate Influence (others acting on your content) and Outreach (your activity) measures; founder-written description.
why_it_matters: A two-number design (influence received vs. activity given) that is worth copying for people ranking; the shutdown is NOT verified by our search.
numbers: Influence scale 1-1000 (founder post, 2012). Shutdown date not confirmed from our search.
ui_notes: Two-score layout: influence received and outreach given, shown side by side.
note: Status unknown; treat as defunct only after a primary source. Founder source, so promotional.

name: Famous Birthdays popularity ranking
what: Celebrity directory whose popularity list is driven by user boosts and likes, with a separate Trending list for recent boost spikes.
why_it_matters: A crowd-vote popularity signal; shows what a user-activity rank looks like at scale.
numbers: About 3 million uniques and 11 million page views a month in 2014 (OMR/SoCal Tech coverage; traffic, not ranking input).
ui_notes: Show Trending and All-time as two different tabs; label the signal as votes.
note: Biases: fan-base mobilization, young and US-skewed user base, vote manipulation; ranking not validated.

name: gitstar-ranking (k0kubun)
what: Open-source (MIT) self-hosted app that ranks GitHub users, organizations and repositories via the GitHub API.
why_it_matters: Reference implementation for a developer-side rank we can rebuild from GitHub API data; the people-graph has repo owners to feed it.
numbers: About 811 stars and 85 forks at capture (gittrend listing).
ui_notes: Show rank as a position with followers and stars as the displayed inputs.
note: Biases: GitHub-only; follower counts reward self-promotion; the ranking formula was not read in this slice (check the repo README).

name: Star History top-committer rank (GitHub commits)
what: Badge that ranks GitHub users among the top committers to the 20,000 most-starred repos and among the 20,000 most-followed users, based on public commit-contribution counts.
why_it_matters: A contribution-count rank that is an alternative to star or follower-based scores; directly usable for repo owners in our graph.
numbers: Universe: 20,000 most-followed users; 20,000 most-starred repos (Star History pages dated 2026-09-14).
ui_notes: Show the badge only when in the universe; say the universe in the caption.
note: Biases: commit counts reward bots and big-org monorepo contributors; universe is capped at the most-followed and most-starred.

name: Top contributors to GitHub 2017 (Felipe Hoffa)
what: Ranking of top GitHub contributors by PushEvent counts grouped by organization, limited to repos with at least 20 stars that year.
why_it_matters: A worked example of building a contributor rank from GH Archive events; reproducible with our own data pipeline.
numbers: Threshold: repos with at least 20 stars in the year (article). Counts per user from PushEvents.
ui_notes: Show a per-org grouping so a single company does not dominate.
note: Biases: push count rewards bots and automation; org grouping hides individuals; 2017 data, old.

name: OSS Insight (PingCAP) repository rankings
what: Real-time repository collection rankings from 10 billion GitHub events, ranking repos by stars, PRs, issues and PR creators over the last 28 days, with yearly history back to 2011.
why_it_matters: Event-based rolling-window ranking pattern to copy for works (repos) and for people (PR creators).
numbers: 10 billion GitHub events; 28-day window; history since 2011 (collection pages). No developer-ranking formula found in search.
ui_notes: Show three metrics as tabs over a 28-day window and a yearly view.
note: Biases: recent-window bias; collections chosen by the site; no developer formula checked.

name: Round-robin pairwise LLM judging with Bradley-Terry (arXiv 2502.14074)
what: Shows round-robin pairwise judging plus Bradley-Terry reduces non-transitivity and gives rankings that match Chatbot Arena human rankings better than fixed baselines.
why_it_matters: The method to rank people or works by LLM judgement without an O(N) baseline bias; applicable to a head-to-head judge of notable people.
numbers: Position switching cuts non-transitivity effects by 17% to 44% for stronger judges (paper summary in search).
ui_notes: Show the rank as a Bradley-Terry score with a 95% interval, not a point.
note: Biases: judge model's own knowledge and training data (Western, English and recent); position bias; verbosity and self-preference bias. Cost O(N squared) pairs, so use sampling.

name: Judging the Judges: systematic study of position bias in pairwise LLM-as-a-judge (arXiv 2406.07791)
what: Systematic study of position bias across many LLM judges and candidate pairs; finds bias is systematic and depends on quality gap between candidates.
why_it_matters: Required reading before any LLM-as-judge people ranking: the bias is not random noise and does not vanish with prompt length changes.
numbers: Across about 12 to 15 judges and about 40 candidate models (summary in search; verify exact numbers in paper).
ui_notes: Show a position-consistency rate next to any LLM-judged rank.
note: Bias: position bias; quality-gap dependence means close pairs flip more.

name: TrueSkill and Elo for pairwise ranking (no people-notability use found)
what: Rating systems that treat each item as a distribution (TrueSkill: mean plus variance) and update on pairwise outcomes; TrueSkill supports multi-player and new items without recomputing others.
why_it_matters: A way to turn human pairwise judgments of people into a rank with uncertainty; no notability study using it was found.
numbers: TrueSkill: mean and variance per player (Wikipedia). GitRanking (arXiv 2205.09379) uses it for GitHub topics with active sampling.
ui_notes: Show a rank plus an uncertainty band that narrows as votes accumulate.
note: Biases: rater pool (who votes), familiarity bias (people vote for names they know), and Elo misspecification under model error (arXiv 2502.10985).

name: NameRank: measuring recognition of people and entities in LLMs (arXiv 2607.12520)
what: Probes 4,685 entities across 36 models with one question each; an independent judge scores whether the model states a specific, checkable fact; yields a [0,1] recognition score.
why_it_matters: A model-side fame measure that can be cross-checked against Wikipedia and pageview ranks, and shows bibliometrics explain little of recognition.
numbers: 4,685 entities, 54 cohorts, 36 models; citations explain about a third of recognition; Nobel, Turing, Fields laureates saturate (abstract, Jul 2026).
ui_notes: Use as a second axis: model recognition vs. our composite.
note: Biases: LLM training-data bias (English, Western, recent); gender inference in the paper relies on Western-name dictionaries and drops many East Asian names.

name: Trump Twitter Archive
what: Searchable archive of @realDonaldTrump tweets, including deleted ones captured from Sept 2016.
why_it_matters: Best-known single-person tweet archive with deletion capture. Good template for the tweet-level record (date, device, deleted flag) that we need for Elon.
numbers: About 56,000 tweets from 2009 (secondary report, qz.com era, unverified current count). Deleted-tweet capture from Sept 2016 (same secondary source).
ui_notes: Search and filter by date and posting device (per secondary reporting). Our fetch returned only the title, so layout is unverified.
note: Current site status unconfirmed; the site returned only a title on fetch. Check the Wayback snapshot before relying on it.

name: bpb27/trump_tweet_data_archive
what: Machine-readable JSON archive of Trump tweets, zipped by year, refreshed hourly.
why_it_matters: A bulk-downloadable schema we can copy: id_str, created_at, source (device), text, favorite and retweet counts. Gives us a field list for Elon rows.
numbers: Files cover 2009 to 2018 by filename (master_2009.json.zip to condensed_2018.json.zip). Repo shows 10,191 commits (not tweets). Tweet count not stated on page.
ui_notes: No UI. Data-only. Condensed vs master files; master holds full API response.
note: No deleted-tweet flag seen in the sample record. Last-commit date and license not shown on the page. | check: GitHub commits API: last page 10,191 commits (matches row); repo 203 stars, 25 forks.

name: Internet Archive TV News Search
what: Search of closed-caption text across US TV news broadcasts, with clips you can borrow and watch.
why_it_matters: Spoken-word TV record for Musk appearances on news channels, with station and time. Captions are real-time and error-prone, so 'Musk' may be misspelled in the index.
numbers: Launch 2012: 350,000 broadcasts (blog.archive.org). A later, less-established site claims 4,430,000 broadcasts from mid-2009 (unverified).
ui_notes: Search by caption phrase; filter by network, show and time window; short streaming clip per hit. Our fetch returned only the title, so result layout is unverified.
note: Caption-based, so a quote here is a transcript line with a station and time, not a verified text of what was said. | check: archive.org advancedsearch collection:tvnews numFound 4,580,741 today; row's 4,430,000 (from a secondary site) is within 10%; the 350,000 at 2012 launch was not checked.

name: Wikiquote: Elon Musk
what: Community quote page grouped by year, with venue, date and link to tweets, interviews, books and speeches.
why_it_matters: The best free per-year citation pattern for Musk on a public page. Already in the blind map as Wikiquote basics; this row adds the citation format it uses.
numbers: About 200 quotes in the visible main section, plus a few in 'Quotes about Musk' (page truncated at 100k chars of 107,633). The 2007 section alone has about 40 quotes from archived pages on evancarmichael.com (fetched page).
ui_notes: Quotes under year headings; each entry names venue (interview, podcast, book, speech, article, tweet) and a date (day-month-year, or year only). Citations link to the source or an archived copy, or cite a news report. Notes flag later deletions. Example: tweet dated 19 Nov 2017 with link; Axios interview 25 Nov 2018 (season 1, episode 4).
note: Many entries cite secondary news rather than the original, and some tweets have no link ('Post on X'). Not exhaustive; we cannot tell which entries are complete.

name: Quote Investigator (Musk-tagged pages)
what: Attribution research articles on quotes credited to Musk, with dated write-ups and a verdict on origin.
why_it_matters: Shows the verification standard we want on a quote record: earliest known source, dated, with apocryphal flags. Three Musk pages listed.
numbers: 3 Musk-tagged articles on the tag page: 2017-09-24 (updated 2025-04-14) on 'mud ball' extinction line; 2019-08-29 (updated 2025-04-04) on simulation; 2023-11-19 (updated 2024-01-20) on small fortune. Verdicts not visible in tag excerpts.
ui_notes: Each article: title, date, updated date, 'Apocryphal?' questions, then origin with earliest known citations. Tag page lists title and date only.
note: Coverage of Musk is thin (3 pages). Use as a method, not a source of Musk quotes.

name: Snopes fact-check: Musk education vs intelligence quote
what: Fact-check of a viral Musk quote: searched for any tweet or statement, found none, traced earlier similar wording.
why_it_matters: Shows how a missing quote is handled: 'no record found' plus earliest similar wording (a 1977 newspaper column). Our record needs a 'not found' status, not silence.
numbers: No record of the quote in Musk's tweets or statements (per search summary of Snopes). 1977 newspaper column as earliest similar wording.
ui_notes: Article text with verdict; no per-quote archive view.
note: Read only via search snippet, not full fetch.

name: Birdwatch Archive
what: Archive of X Birdwatch community notes, each linked to the post it annotates by ID.
why_it_matters: Keeps fact-check notes on posts, which can outlive deleted posts. A possible side source for Musk posts that were later edited or removed.
numbers: Not counted (fetch of the home page timed out). One 2023 note says Musk's tweets were searchable on mobile via from:elonmusk at that time (unverified).
ui_notes: Note page with the note text and the linked post ID; date shown on the note.
note: Notes are user-written, so they are pointers, not verdicts. Post embeds are no longer reliable.

name: Zenodo: Auditing Elon Musk's Impact on Hate Speech and Bots (datasets)
what: Research dataset of tweet IDs and daily counts around Musk's Oct-Nov 2022 ownership period, plus hate-word tweets.
why_it_matters: A citable Musk-tweet dataset with IDs and dates. Can be used to recover text for IDs we hold, and to check our 92k Zenodo CSVs for gaps in 2022.
numbers: Data 197.5 MB total. Tweet-ID files cover 2022; hate-level file covers 2022-10-01 to 2022-11-30. Record count not stated on page. Views 170, downloads 22 at fetch.
ui_notes: Data only: CSV tweet IDs with dates; frequency CSVs; Perspective API attribute columns on hate-word tweets (names not listed).
note: Text and engagement not included in ID files. Files restricted and require login to check access (per fetch). CC BY 4.0.

name: Kaggle: Elon Musk tweets Jan-Oct 2022 (via secondary analysis)
what: Kaggle-hosted Musk tweet CSVs (2021 tweets paired with Dogecoin prices; a 2022 set covering 27 Jan to 27 Oct 2022).
why_it_matters: Public, free Musk tweet CSVs with timestamp and tweet ID. Good for overlap checks with our Zenodo set.
numbers: 2022 set covers 27 Jan to 27 Oct 2022 at about 11 tweets per day (per a secondary analysis). Row counts not verified.
ui_notes: Kaggle dataset page: file preview table.
note: Kaggle itself returned only a title on fetch; the URL is a third-party mirror. Coverage gaps likely.

name: Gumroad: elon tweets (paid CSV)
what: Paid CSV of Musk tweets with ID, text, date and engagement counts.
why_it_matters: Only off-the-shelf Musk set with engagement fields we found; claims more than 20,000 tweets. Compare with our 92k before paying.
numbers: Claims 20,000+ tweets (listing); search summary says 20200+ rows at $0.99. Collection method not stated.
ui_notes: Product listing page; file preview not available to us.
note: Not fetched; provenance unknown. Treat as unverified. | check: lowbyte.gumroad.com listing shows '20200+ elon musk tweets' (matches); the $0.99 price was not visible in the fetched page.

name: YouGlish
what: Pronunciation search over YouTube clips for a word or phrase.
why_it_matters: Not a person archive. Listed only to rule it out for 'what did X say'.
numbers: 25 language options; English accent filters (US, UK, AU, CA, IE, SCO, NZ). No coverage count on page.
ui_notes: Phrase search returning short video clips; context tags such as #Obama appear.
note: Out of scope for person archives; included to close the question.

name: Listen Notes podcast search and API
what: Podcast search engine with an API; transcripts available as an option on episode lookup.
why_it_matters: Lets us search podcast episodes for a person's name and pull episode metadata at scale. Transcript coverage is the limit.
numbers: About 3.3M podcasts and 190M+ episodes; free tier 300 requests/month; commercial around $200/month (GTM Directory, secondary, approximate).
ui_notes: API docs; search returns episodes with publish date and podcast name; transcript via episode endpoint option (per tutorial).
note: Figures from a third-party directory, not Listen Notes itself. Confirm pricing on their pricing page. | check: listennotes.com API pricing (en): free tier is 150 requests/month, not 300; $200/month base fee for 1+ requests matches the row's commercial figure.

name: Taddy podcast API (and Podcast Index comparison)
what: Podcast API vendor whose blog says Podcast Index has no episode search and transcripts exist for under 1% of its episodes.
why_it_matters: Sets the realistic ceiling on free podcast transcripts: most open feeds have no transcript. Transcripts are a paid feature on Taddy.
numbers: Podcast Index transcripts for under 1% of episodes (competitor claim). Taddy developers page: transcripts and webhooks are paid.
ui_notes: API; episode objects; transcript endpoint (paid).
note: Competitor marketing source; verify against Podcast Index docs before use.

name: Huberman Lab official transcripts (Premium) and PodcastRex
what: Official episode transcripts behind a paid tier, searchable by topic, guest and keyword in the dashboard; third-party PodcastRex transcripts with speaker labels.
why_it_matters: A creator-run transcript index with search, so it is a model for a single-person archive. Shows the paid-gate reality for a person's own archive.
numbers: PodcastRex lists 30 of 794 Huberman episodes transcribed (free preview).
ui_notes: Official dashboard lists transcripts by episode type and date, with a search bar (topic, guest, keyword); transcript tab on each episode page. PodcastRex: speaker-labelled transcript per episode.
note: Huberman is not a person in our slice; included as the best single-creator transcript index pattern.

name: Lex Fridman transcript sources (transcript.lol; Lexicap)
what: Third-party Whisper-style transcripts of Lex Fridman episodes; transcript.lol lists user-requested episodes only.
why_it_matters: Lex Fridman's long-form interviews include many Musk appearances; a per-episode transcript is the raw input for dated quotes.
numbers: transcript.lol: 13 items (per search summary). Lexicap: described as Whisper transcripts for all episodes, but the karpathy.ai page we fetched did not describe the project.
ui_notes: transcript.lol: per-episode transcript page, request-a-transcript form. Lexicap: zip of raw captions (per search summary).
note: Lexicap URL did not confirm on fetch (returned Karpathy homepage). Treat Lexicap as unverified.

name: Paul Graham essay index (paulgraham.com)
what: Complete list of Paul Graham essays on one page.
why_it_matters: A clean full-corpus list for a single author, but undated on the index. Shows that even good archives often lack a date at the list level.
numbers: About 235 entries, about 233 essays plus 2 book chapters (manual count). Only explicit year on the page: 1998 (Viaweb snapshot).
ui_notes: Plain title list; each link goes to an essay that carries its own date line.
note: Essays are the author's own writing, not spoken quotes; included as a 'complete corpus' benchmark. | check: paulgraham.com/articles.html: 246 unique .html links, which includes a few non-essay pages; row says about 235 entries (within 10%).

name: Quotewise (Naval Ravikant tweet-style quotes)
what: Quote aggregator with one page per line, each carrying a source attribution; premium advanced filters by source and date.
why_it_matters: Only per-person quote archive we found for Naval; no official nav.al search. Shows the risk: a quote-check of seven popular Naval lines found 6 with no original located and 1 with no reliable source.
numbers: Not counted. Secondary check: 6 of 7 popular lines consistently credited but original not located; 1 with no reliable source.
ui_notes: One page per quote with source line; premium search filters by source, date and more.
note: Borderline generic quote site; kept only for the per-person source pattern. Fact-check source for the 6-of-7 claim not fetched.

what: Creator behind t3.gg. Covers the T3 stack, T3 Code (pingdotgg), SnitchBench (LLM benchmark) and commentary on other builders. T3 Chat was named in the brief but no source was found for it.
why_it_matters: SnitchBench is a reproducible method-style benchmark (reproduced publicly by Simon Willison). T3 Code is the most-starred item in this slice and is a coding-agent control plane. The video stream is mostly commentary, so pull by pick.
numbers: YouTube @t3dotgg: 551K subs (SpeakRJ, 2026-07-17), 561K (Social Blade, undated), 571K (OutlierKit, undated); 1,105 videos and ~108M views (SpeakRJ, 2026-07-17). T3 Chat: no source found. | check: GitHub figures match (t3code 27,432 stars; t3dotgg 20,506 followers / 135 repos; pingdotgg 1,846 / 14).
